text:
TSMC's "1nm Advancement" vs. Samsung Electronics' "2nm Stabilization"

Amid the AI boom, Taiwan's leading foundry TSMC is drawing attention for its focused efforts to advance its sub-nanometer foundry process roadmap. TSMC plans to enter the 1-nanometer (nm) node next year and commercialize progressively advanced derivative nodes every year thereafter. In contrast, Samsung Electronics is reportedly focusing on optimizing its 2nm process rather than pushing aggressively into more advanced nodes — a relatively cautious approach to leading-edge process development.

According to industry sources on the 27th, the sub-nanometer foundry strategies of Samsung Electronics and TSMC are expected to diverge significantly starting at the 1nm node.

TSMC unveiled its leading-edge foundry process roadmap during its recent Q1 earnings call and North America Technology Symposium. According to the disclosure, TSMC will begin volume production of its 1nm-class advanced node in 2027, starting with "A16." The "A" stands for Angstrom (0.1 nanometer), so A16 corresponds to 1.6nm.

TSMC then plans to mass-produce A14 in 2028 and A13 in 2029. A13, newly disclosed this month, delivers a 6% area reduction compared to A14. It is also reported to feature improved power efficiency and performance through DTCO (Design-Technology Co-Optimization).

The next-generation A12 is also targeted for 2029 mass production. Based on A14, A12 is characterized by the application of "Super Power Rail," a backside power delivery network (BSPDN) technology aimed at the AI and high-performance computing (HPC) industries. BSPDN is a technology that separates signal processing and power delivery — both of which were previously placed on the front side of the wafer — by relocating the power delivery network to the wafer's backside.

Samsung Electronics, TSMC's main competitor, is taking a somewhat different strategy. Samsung had previously prioritized process miniaturization, becoming the world's first to mass-produce a 3nm node based on GAA (Gate-All-Around) architecture in 2022.

However, at last year's "SAFE Forum," where the company unveiled its foundry process roadmap, Samsung pushed back its 1.4nm (SF1.4) mass production target by approximately two years — from the originally planned 2027 to 2029. Rather than aggressively entering the 1nm node, Samsung's strategy is to focus on optimizing and advancing existing nodes such as 2nm.

The industry expects Samsung to once again present a strategy centered on the 2nm process at this year's SAFE Forum, scheduled to be held in the U.S. in late May.

A system semiconductor industry source said, "Samsung has yet to present a definitive picture of its post-2nm process roadmap. With 2nm utilization expected to rise significantly through the acquisition of both internal and external customers, the company is currently devoting all its efforts to optimization and yield improvement."

"Apple to Become World's #3 Notebook Vendor This Year"... Driven by MacBook Neo and Unified Memory Architecture

Apple is projected to overtake Dell to claim the #3 spot in global notebook shipments this year, driven by the recently launched entry-level MacBook Neo and its Unified Memory Architecture (UMA). The global notebook market is expected to contract 8% this year, with Lenovo and Dell — both armed with strong memory procurement leverage — likely to outperform peers.

On the 26th, market research firm Sigmaintell forecast that global notebook shipments this year will fall 8% to 181.1 million units, down from 196.7 million units last year. The decline reflects rising component prices, particularly memory chips, alongside broader market weakness.

Vendor-level shipment forecasts for this year are as follows: Lenovo 43 million units, HP 39 million, Apple 28 million, Dell 22.5 million, Asus 16.5 million, Acer 10.9 million, and others 21.2 million.

Apple is the sole major vendor expected to post growth, with shipments rising 22% from 23 million units last year to 28 million this year. Every other major vendor is projected to decline year-over-year. Dell's shipments are expected to drop from 24.2 million to 22.5 million units, allowing Apple to leapfrog Dell into third place.

Apple has rounded out its MacBook lineup this year with the launch of the entry-level MacBook Neo. The previous MacBook lineup consisted of the Pro and Air, both priced above the Neo. The MacBook Neo starts at 990,000 won.

Sigmaintell also highlighted Apple's Unified Memory Architecture (UMA). UMA is a design unique to Apple Silicon in which the CPU and GPU share memory resources. According to Sigmaintell, Apple has standardized memory specifications across multiple product lines, improving flexibility in component sourcing.

Apple's revenue model is another differentiating factor. Apple generates substantial services revenue from the App Store, iCloud, and similar offerings, meaning it does not need to fully pass through memory price increases into finished-product pricing. Apple uses hardware like the MacBook as an "entry point" into its ecosystem, with services revenue offsetting hardware-side cost pressure.

Sigmaintell noted that Apple's revenue model differentiates it from x86-camp Windows notebook vendors that rely on Intel and AMD CPUs. The x86 camp is heavily dependent on hardware sales. While Apple's notebook shipment forecast trails Lenovo and others, per-unit profit and overall margins are expected to exceed those of peers.

Within the x86 camp, fortunes are expected to diverge this year due to differences in memory procurement power. Lenovo and Dell, both with sizable server businesses, are expected to outperform, while Asus and Acer — with minimal server market share — face greater headwinds. Servers consume far more memory per unit than notebooks, so a larger server business translates into stronger memory procurement leverage. Securing memory in bulk at relatively lower prices helps ease cost pressure on the notebook side.

All major x86 notebook vendors are expected to see shipment declines this year, but the magnitude varies. Lenovo, with its high server market share, is forecast to decline 6% (45.6 million → 43 million units), and Dell 7% (24.2 million → 22.5 million units) — both narrower than the overall market's expected 8% decline.

In contrast, HP is projected to decline 11% (43.7 million → 39 million units), Asus 10% (18.4 million → 16.5 million units), and Acer 15% (12.9 million → 10.9 million units) — all steeper than the broader market. Acer's heavy reliance on low-end products is a particular drag.

Combined shipments from vendors outside this top tier are expected to plunge 27%, from 28.9 million units last year to 21.2 million units this year.

Jukan's Truth Time:

Many people have been asking:

"Samsung has its own DRAM division — so why isn't it aggressively pursuing mobile device market share expansion during a memory shortage like this?"

Today, I'll give you the answer.

First, let me clear up a common misconception.

Samsung's MX (Galaxy division) and Samsung's DS division (semiconductor division) only share the Samsung name — they do not share a single, unified interest. Each puts its own profits first.

This became clear in what happened before Samsung MX launched the Galaxy S25.

At the time, Samsung MX concluded that the LPDDR5X built on Samsung's 1b node lagged behind the offerings from SK Hynix and Micron in both performance and thermals. Yet Samsung DS was trying to sell this underperforming LPDDR5X to Samsung MX at a higher price than SK Hynix's and Micron's LPDDR5X.

This led to an unprecedented outcome: Micron — not Samsung — became the first vendor for the mobile DRAM in Samsung's flagship S-series smartphones. (TM Roh, head of Samsung MX, later denied this. But for at least the initial-to-mid production volumes, Micron has been confirmed as the first vendor.)

Now, however, the situation is reversed. As the term "Memorypocalypse" floating around the market suggests, memory is currently in extreme short supply.

So — after going through what happened in 2025, would Samsung DS really turn around and supply LPDDR5X to MX at a discount?

Another interesting point: one of the reasons MX cannot source DRAM cheaply from DS is that DS has to be mindful of its external customers.

Specifically, if Samsung supplies DRAM to its internal divisions at a discount, its external customers — who are already paying steep prices for DRAM — would be deeply unhappy. Trust between Samsung and its customers would break down, and customers would hold a grudge against Samsung.

Samsung DS reportedly has no appetite for taking on that kind of risk.

As a result, Samsung MX, having already incurred massive costs in Q1 due to difficulty securing memory and a sharp rise in its procurement prices, is expected to spend even more in Q2 to meet its volume requirements as the world's largest mobile device manufacturer.

This aligns with reports that TM Roh, head of Samsung MX, has briefed management that MX could swing to a loss this year.

In conclusion, the reason Samsung MX cannot aggressively pursue a market share expansion strategy during this memory shortage is not simply that "Samsung has a DRAM division but can't make use of it."

The core reasons are threefold:

First, MX and DS sit under the same Samsung roof, but their interests diverge. Second, DS has no choice but to prioritize its own profitability and its external customer relationships over internal supply. Third, in the current memory shortage environment, MX — like any external customer — is structurally forced to bear elevated memory costs.

That's all for today's Jukan's Truth Time. Thank you.

The most interesting comment I read in today’s report:

All of Anthropic's unusual moves around the GPT-5.5 launch ultimately converge on a single conclusion: in order to secure compute, Anthropic must bind itself far more deeply — and far more dependently — to those who possess these physical resources. This conclusion was crystallized in the $100B deal formalized a few days ago. The most representative example is the deal with Amazon. The key terms are as follows:

- Amazon will inject an additional $5B into Anthropic immediately, with up to $20B more in follow-on investment to come. Combined with the existing $8B, cumulative investment reaches up to $33B.
- Up to 5GW of compute capacity secured, of which roughly 1GW is scheduled to come online by year-end 2026.
- Anthropic has committed to spending $100B+ on AWS technology over the next 10 years (including usage requirements for AWS silicon such as Trainium and Graviton).
- Purchase rights secured for Trainium2/3/4 and future Trainium generations. Trainium2 is currently sold out, and Trainium3 is largely booked as well.
- The Claude Platform will be offered natively on AWS.

Just how large is the 5GW Anthropic has committed to? It is equivalent to roughly five nuclear power plants. Given that Microsoft's total global data center footprint in 2024 is estimated at around 5–6GW, this means Anthropic alone is locking in incremental capacity — for AI training and serving — that rivals the entirety of MSFT's historical physical infrastructure. Coupled with Anthropic's announcement of having reached $30B ARR, the market is reading this deal as "Anthropic pre-signing Amazon's invoice in order to keep its growth going."

It is also worth noting Dario Amodei's (Anthropic CEO) remarks accompanying the announcement: "Users tell us that Claude is becoming increasingly essential to how they work. We need to build infrastructure to keep up with rapidly growing demand." Last month's blog post from Anthropic — directly admitting that "surging enterprise/developer demand is placing unavoidable strain on our infrastructure, affecting reliability and performance" — was effectively a teaser for this deal.

What matters is that the structure of this deal is more favorable to Amazon than to Anthropic. Amazon has already invested in OpenAI as well (up to $50B). In other words, the more fiercely OpenAI and Anthropic compete to eat each other's lunch, the more Amazon benefits simultaneously along three axes: cloud usage fees from both, adoption rates for its in-house silicon (Trainium as XPU, Graviton as CPU), and visibility on the recovery of data center CAPEX. This is structurally almost identical to the valuation premium Google historically enjoyed under the "full-stack player" framing.

The market, however, has not yet fully come around to recognizing Amazon in this light. (Sentiment has admittedly improved compared to two weeks ago.) Amazon is still trading near a 10-year low on CY26 EV/EBITDA. But as the rivalry between the two AI labs escalates and Amazon begins to collect its "toll-gate revenue," we believe the market is likely to gradually move toward a re-rating.

(Excerpt from Mirae Asset Securities’ AI Hot Issue report, dated April 24, 2026)

"Samsung Union Strike Could Disrupt Memory Mass Production for At Least 1 Month"… Industry Concerns Mount

Labor-management conflict at Samsung Electronics is intensifying over the size of performance bonuses. The Samsung Group Cho-gi-eop Union's Samsung Electronics chapter (hereinafter "the union") reaffirmed on the 23rd at a resolution rally its intent to push ahead with an 18-day general strike starting on the 21st of next month.

On the 25th, concerns emerged within the semiconductor industry that the Samsung Electronics union strike could have a significant ripple effect on the memory semiconductor market.

While the union has announced an 18-day strike period, when factoring in the time required to bring equipment back online to normal operating conditions, production disruption could last at least one month or more. The impact on mass production stretches to at least double that period. There are also forecasts that, amid the memory supercycle, only Samsung Electronics' competitors will reap windfall benefits.

One semiconductor engineer explained, "If setup and maintenance (CS) work on semiconductor equipment is suspended for an extended period, restoring equipment to normal operation can take more than a month," adding, "The impact could be even greater in a supercycle situation where memory shipments need to be aggressively ramped up."

The union strike is not an issue confined to Samsung Electronics alone. If Samsung Electronics—which holds the world's largest production capacity—experiences disruptions in mass production, the memory supply crunch could worsen further. For global Big Tech and IT companies, this means greater pressure from rising manufacturing costs.

In such a scenario, competitors such as SK Hynix and Micron could enjoy the windfall of a steeper rise in memory prices. Volatility is expected to be particularly pronounced in high-performance server DRAM and eSSD (enterprise SSD) segments, where only a handful of companies are capable of mass production.

Another semiconductor engineer said, "When personnel are pulled out of the fab, equipment starts going offline one by one, creating problems," and added, "If memory equipment isn't properly managed, output can immediately drop by 10–20%."

The union is demanding that 15% of annual operating profit be distributed as performance bonuses and that the bonus system be made more transparent. Approximately 40,000 people (police estimate) gathered at the resolution rally held on the 23rd at Samsung Electronics' Pyeongtaek campus, where the same message was emphasized. More than half of the 76,100 members of Samsung Electronics' first-ever majority union in the company's history attended the rally. If a labor-management agreement is not reached, the union will proceed with a general strike.

At the rally, Union Chairman Choi Seung-ho warned, "If the company treats devoted union members as mere numbers, we too will respond with numbers—by demonstrating the massive production disruptions and losses that a strike will cause." Estimated losses from the strike have been pegged at up to 30 trillion won.

Thoughts after reading the DeepSeek V4 paper:

- NVIDIA really is something else. Remember how back in 2024 people were bashing Blackwell as overspec'd and dismissing FP4 as just marketing? Turns out it was all groundwork for the next generation of models. Maybe NVIDIA's moat is its ability to anticipate the trajectory of mainstream LLM technology and the new demands on accelerators 3–5 years out, plan and position accordingly, and bake that foresight into product design. Other GPU companies don't anticipate demand — they react to it.

- Have NVIDIA and DeepSeek been talking to each other? Looking at the 6144 FLOPs/Byte passage — I'd been wondering why NVIDIA was pushing HBM4 pin speeds up so aggressively, and it turns out raising Rubin's HBM4 pin speed isn't "overkill" from the perspective of a model like V4. It's a precisely balanced design.

- NVIDIA is once again working hard to crank up bandwidth on Rubin Ultra, which is telling: it implies that Rubin Ultra's FP4 compute is getting too fast relative to HBM bandwidth, and that HBM bandwidth could once again become the bottleneck when training MoE models like DeepSeek-V4.

- Why is the next-gen NVIDIA chip scaling up the NVL domain? Why are they moving toward Kyber? You can read this as an attempt to push up the bandwidth-density of the interconnect fabric, pulling compute — which has surged above the threshold — back into a communication-friendly balance.

text:
[EXCLUSIVE] Samsung Breaks DRAM's "10nm Wall"... First Working Die Produced

Samsung Electronics is breaking through the DRAM 10nm wall.

The company has produced the world's first working die (a functioning prototype) of a single-digit-nanometer DRAM. Samsung is reportedly planning to rapidly secure yield by tuning process conditions based on this working die.

According to industry sources on the 24th, Samsung confirmed a working die last month during die characterization testing of wafers produced on its 10a process. The result was the company's first-ever application of a 4F² cell structure combined with Vertical Channel Transistor (VCT) process technology.

The DRAM industry has traditionally classified its 10nm-class generations in the sequence 1x → 1y → 1z → 1a → 1b → 1c → 1d. The 10a node, the generation following 1d, refers to the first node below 10nm. Experts estimate the actual circuit linewidth to be around 9.5–9.7nm.

A "working die" refers to a chip cut from a wafer that operates as designed. When a working die emerges during development, it signals that the design and process direction are correct. From there, the effort shifts to yield ramp and reliability qualification.

Samsung plans to complete 10a DRAM development this year using this architecture, move to quality testing next year, and transfer it to mass-production lines in 2028. The company reportedly intends to apply the 4F² and VCT structure across three generations — 10a, 10b, and 10c — before transitioning to 3D DRAM starting from 10d.

An industry source said, "Samsung had also kept a separate team designing the next-next-generation DRAM under the conventional approach, out of concern that the 10a process could fail. But now that a working die has been produced, development and commercialization using this technology will move into high gear."

The reason failure concerns had been high is that 4F² and VCT are brand-new technologies.

Until now, DRAM cell area has been based on 6F². With 10a, this shrinks to 4F². A 6F² structure has a rectangular cell measuring 3F horizontally by 2F vertically (area = 6F²), while 4F² is a square, 2F on each side (area = 4F²). Moving to 4F² theoretically allows 30–50% more cells to be packed into the same die size, delivering advantages in capacity, speed, and power consumption.

The challenge was how to arrange the gate, channel, and capacitor on top of this narrower cell area. Samsung addressed this by introducing VCT technology. VCT is a structure in which the capacitor, which stores charge, is stacked on top of the transistor. In conventional designs, the transistor and capacitor each occupied their own cell area. Peripheral circuits such as sense amplifiers, test circuits, timing controllers, and voltage regulators — which had traditionally been placed around the cell array — are reportedly being processed on a separate wafer and attached via wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding using a PUC (Periphery Under Cell) approach.

With 4F² and VCT technology applied, key materials have also changed. Samsung has switched the channel material from silicon to Indium Gallium Zinc Oxide (IGZO). The channel is the pathway through which current flows in a transistor. IGZO was adopted to suppress leakage current in the shrunken cell and secure data retention characteristics.

The wordline material is still in flux. The wordline is the interconnect that selects cells during DRAM operation. Samsung's original plan was to switch from conventional titanium nitride (TiN) to molybdenum (Mo). Molybdenum offers low resistance and does not require a liner layer during deposition, which widens the current path at the same linewidth. However, it is highly corrosive and solid at room temperature, which means gas supply equipment and piping must be modified for mass production. Process control difficulty is also high. Because of this, the option of extending TiN usage has recently re-emerged. Adoption probabilities for the two options are currently said to be roughly 50/50.

An industry source explained, "A structure in which VCT is laid on its side and stacked is essentially 3D DRAM, so Samsung has effectively laid the technological groundwork. Micron and Chinese DRAM makers plan to skip 4F² and VCT and go directly to 3D DRAM."

Micron plans to stretch its existing design as far as possible. Chinese DRAM makers, unable to import EUV lithography equipment, cannot shrink linewidths by any conventional means under current conditions. However, viewing 3D DRAM as a way to produce leading-edge products using legacy lithography — much like 3D NAND flash — they are aggressively pursuing 3D DRAM development.

SK Hynix is reportedly planning to apply 4F² and VCT technology at its 10b node rather than at 10a.

urls.description: Google's unveiling of its eighth-generation tensor processing unit (TPU) at Cloud Next 2026 is expected to drive the next wave of growth in the application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) server supply chain, with Taiwanese manufacturers expanding their role, according to supply chain sources.

text:
Exclusive: Google ramps new TPU servers, Taiwan suppliers gain share

Google's unveiling of its eighth-generation tensor processing unit (TPU) at Cloud Next 2026 is expected to drive the next wave of growth in the application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) server supply chain, with Taiwanese manufacturers expanding their role, according to supply chain sources.

Assembly partners, including Celestica and Foxconn, are expected to begin volume production in the second half of 2026. Key component suppliers such as Asia Vital Components and Cooler Master are preparing shipments by the end of the second quarter, with Inventec reportedly set to begin production earlier.

Taiwan gains share across supply chain
Taiwanese vendors are taking on a larger role in Google's TPU server ecosystem. While Broadcom has historically dominated upstream IC design, MediaTek has also entered the supply chain, according to sources.

In server motherboard production, Inventec's share is reportedly rising from about 10 to 30%, gradually taking orders from Celestica. The companies declined to comment.

Supply chain sources said Taiwanese firms remain competitive in terms of flexibility, quality, and pricing, supported by long-standing experience in server manufacturing. Inventec is currently the world's second-largest server motherboard supplier.

ASIC servers to outpace GPU growth
ASIC servers are expected to be the fastest-growing segment of the AI server market in 2026, outpacing systems based on GPUs led by Nvidia.

DIGITIMES Research estimates ASIC server shipments will grow 64.2% year-over-year in 2026, compared with 43.8% growth for GPU servers.

Industry sources said rising ASIC shipments are also likely to support demand for general-purpose servers. Google's continued investment in ASIC infrastructure is expected to benefit its primary general server assembler, Quanta Computer, in 2026.

Dual-chip TPU highlights shift to inference
Google's eighth-generation TPU introduces a dual-chip architecture for the first time, separating training and inference workloads.

The lineup includes TPU 8t for large-scale training and TPU 8i for low-latency inference. Both chips are expected to launch later in 2026, with shipments projected before year-end, according to supply chain estimates.

The move reflects a broader shift in AI development. Over the past three years, the industry has focused on large-scale training, but leading chipmakers, including Google and Nvidia, are placing greater emphasis on inference, indicating a widening range of AI applications.

Google remains key ASIC player
Google continues to be a major driver of ASIC-based AI infrastructure. DIGITIMES Research estimates the company will account for 46% of the ASIC accelerator market in 2026, with shipments reaching about 3.33 million units.

The TPU v7, code-named Ironwood, is expected to remain the main product, accounting for 89% of Google's total TPU shipments.

Industry sources said Celestica remains the primary assembly partner for TPU servers, but Taiwanese firms are expanding their role. This is most evident in CPU motherboard production, where Inventec's share is increasing, and in L10 to L11 assembly, where Foxconn is involved.

On the supply side, NAND capacity additions remain measured: SK Hynix's core focus is on technology migration, while new capacity is concentrated in SNDK/Kioxia's K2 fab, Samsung's P5 line (coming online in 2028), and YMTC.

☀️ Cost optimization may reshape the NAND vs. DRAM competitive landscape: We expect the memory market to approach $1 trillion in size by 2027, with CSPs accounting for 40–45% of total demand and memory spend representing over 40% of CSP CAPEX. On this basis, we believe the cost advantage will progressively tilt the revenue mix toward NAND (server DRAM is priced at ~$2.2/Gb, vs. eSSD at just $0.35–0.37/GB). Tiered storage architecture is the core structural driver of rising NAND share in AI workloads, and the arrival of HBF from 2028 onward should further amplify this. Market research firm Sigmaintell announced on the 22nd that Apple will be the only company to show growth in this year's notebook market.

Sigmaintell projects global notebook shipments this year at 181.1 million units, down 8% YoY. The decline is attributed to price increases caused by memory supply shortages and slowing market demand. As a result, all companies except Apple are expected to see negative growth in shipments this year.

Sigmaintell estimates Apple's notebook shipments at 28 million units, up approximately 21.7% YoY, ranking third in notebook shipments. The new launch of the entry-level MacBook Neo is also seen as a positive factor. The product lineup diversification is analyzed to have expanded market demand. In contrast, other companies are expected to bear the full brunt of memory price increases. Market leader Lenovo is projected to ship 43 million units, down 6% YoY—lower than the market average decline of 8%. The analysis suggests that the large-scale memory purchases by Lenovo's server division will work favorably in unit-price negotiations.

Second-place HP is projected at 39 million units, down 11% YoY. Fifth-place ASUS is forecast at 16.5 million units, down 10% YoY, while sixth-place Acer is projected at 10.9 million units, down 15%. Acer has a high proportion of low-end products and a relatively small scale of memory purchases.

Sigmaintell stated, "This year, notebook companies are competing not merely through finished-product competition but with the capabilities of the entire group," adding, "Brands that fail to adapt to this change and remain confined to a single hardware-based revenue structure will be eliminated from the market."

Samsung's P4 Sprint: Mass Production Pulled Forward by Half a Year

Samsung Electronics will bring Fab 4 (P4)—the facility it has been building at its Pyeongtaek campus with a KRW 50 trillion investment to expand its artificial intelligence (AI) memory business—into full operation within this year. The company plans to leverage "temporary use approval" to advance P4's full ramp by roughly six months versus the original schedule. According to industry sources on the 22nd, Samsung Electronics plans to secure temporary use approvals for P4's Sangdong (Ph4) line in July and its Hadong (Ph2) line in November, and commence operations accordingly. Last month, Samsung C&T's Construction division was awarded the P4 Hadong finishing work at KRW 1.3792 trillion, accelerating the final stages of the build. P4, which will house four cleanrooms arranged across two floors, is currently operating at only half capacity.

"Temporary use" refers to obtaining approval for specific zones ahead of full completion in order to bring semiconductor equipment in early. Through this mechanism, P4's full-operation timing will be shortened by about half a year versus the prior schedule. With approximately KRW 50 trillion invested into a single fab, the sequential ramp of P4 within this year is expected to further improve Samsung Electronics' earnings as the company rides the semiconductor supercycle.

Pyeongtaek Fab 5 (P5), which broke ground on structural framework construction last November, entered main construction this month and is likewise accelerating its build pace. P5 is a mammoth-class fab featuring six cleanrooms across three floors, with total investment expected to exceed KRW 80 trillion. Samsung C&T (KRW 2.8932 trillion) and Samsung E&A (KRW 1.8790 trillion) have recently signed large-scale structural framework and construction contracts with Samsung Electronics, putting the project firmly on track.

Samsung is accelerating its pursuit of a "manufacturing super-gap"—on top of its technological lead—in order to respond in a timely manner to surging demand for memory chips including HBM and NAND, driven by products such as NVIDIA's next-generation AI chip "Vera Rubin," which enters mass production in the second half of this year. Samsung Electronics is planning approximately KRW 70 trillion in capex this year, with a significant portion already allocated to the Pyeongtaek campus.

text:
Samsung: $108.1 Billion Poured into P5 Twin Fab… Supplying HBM "More, Faster"

Samsung Electronics has launched an unprecedented production speed campaign, activating a "temporary use" approach at Fab 4 (P4) of its Pyeongtaek Campus and a "Twin Fab" strategy at Fab 5 (P5). With the outlook that the AI semiconductor supercycle will not be a one-off boom but a prolonged phenomenon materializing into reality, this is interpreted as Samsung's decisive bet to completely dominate the AI semiconductor value chain, wielding overwhelming production capacity as its weapon.

The site where capacity will be expanded first is P4. The "temporary use" method Samsung Electronics has decided to apply to the P4 line is an approach whereby use approval for specific zones is obtained before the entire building is completed — allowing cleanroom construction to begin and critical semiconductor equipment to be brought in preemptively. Through this, the physical time required for equipment setup and trial operation can be drastically reduced, pulling operational timing forward by at least six months and increasing chip output.

P5, the next core base, is also focused on speed and efficiency. Samsung plans to construct the new fab that will be built after P5 not as a newly designed P6, but as "P5-2," which will be 100% structurally identical to P5. When semiconductor line designs are changed, major global customers spend several months re-validating product yield and quality. However, when chips are produced in structurally identical twin fabs, complex and time-consuming validation procedures can be skipped, enabling immediate mass supply.

The reason Samsung Electronics is staking everything on such rapid capacity expansion is that the severe memory supply shortage is intensifying. According to foreign media and other sources, the dominant — and bleak — outlook is that even if global memory manufacturers pour all their efforts into fab expansion and production line conversion through next year, they will only be able to satisfy around 60% of surging memory demand. This means the current AI-driven memory supercycle is on a fundamentally different dimension from past volatile cycles led by replacement demand for downstream IT devices such as PCs and smartphones.

Given the situation, leaders of global Big Tech firms and C-level executives overseeing procurement are boarding flights to Korea in succession. They are directly visiting memory manufacturers such as Samsung Electronics and requesting Long-Term Agreements (LTA) in 3-to-5-year units, going on emergency footing to secure stable volumes. An industry source explained, "In a situation where demand is firmly guaranteed and supply is severely insufficient, the company that produces volume first and supplies it at the right time gains an absolute advantage."

Analysts say that by further expanding its already dominant production capacity, Samsung Electronics has seized a golden window to flip the competitive landscape of the High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) market in one stroke. Samsung Electronics reclaimed the top spot in the commodity DRAM market at the end of last year.

The remaining task is dominating the HBM market, where it has ceded the lead to competitors. Expectations are building that, in step with the launch of NVIDIA's next-generation AI accelerator "Vera Rubin," which enters full-scale mass production in the second half of this year, Samsung Electronics will mass-produce HBM4 at the early-activated P4 and reverse market share at once.

The scale of capital being deployed to underpin this speed campaign is equally overwhelming. Given that constructing a single P5 fab alone costs approximately KRW 80 trillion ($54 billion), building the twin fabs (P5, P5-2) is projected to require total funding of more than KRW 160 trillion ($108.1 billion). Indeed, Samsung C&T has disclosed a KRW 2.8932 trillion contract for P5 fab construction and related work, while Samsung E&A has disclosed a KRW 1.879 trillion contract for structural framework construction, announced in succession.

Behind these astronomical investments being executed without wavering lies the robust cash generation capability flowing from record-high earnings. Samsung Electronics posted KRW 57 trillion in operating profit in Q1 of this year alone, setting a record that will be etched into Korean corporate history. According to financial information provider FnGuide, driven by the explosion in AI memory demand, Samsung Electronics' annual operating profit forecast for this year is estimated to reach approximately KRW 319 trillion.

Experts view that Samsung Electronics' turnkey (integrated supply) competitiveness — spanning memory, foundry (semiconductor contract manufacturing), design, and packaging — combined with this capacity expansion, will generate explosive synergy. Kim Yong-seok, Chair Professor at Gachon University's Graduate School of Semiconductors, assessed: "There are even projections that Samsung, having internalized both advanced memory and foundry capabilities, will surpass the heyday of Intel, which dominated the CPU market in the PC era. It has essentially seized the perfect opportunity to newly leap forward as an 'integrated AI semiconductor company.'"

text:
[Exclusive] Iran War Fallout… Japan's Semiconductor Photo Material Supply Chain 'On the Brink of Collapse'

A new flashpoint has emerged in the semiconductor materials supply chain in the wake of the Iran war.

Due to a solvent shortage, the Japanese industry is experiencing disruptions in the overall production of photo process materials, including photoresist (PR). Because Japan holds a high share in photo process materials, concerns are growing that domestic (Korean) semiconductor production could also take a hit.

According to multiple industry sources on the 22nd, major Japanese photo material suppliers have, since the previous evening, either already communicated—or are scheduled to communicate—the raw material sourcing disruptions to semiconductor customers such as Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix through their Korean subsidiaries. One source said, "The Japanese companies that were notified yesterday (the 21st) evening are holding internal meetings today and are scheduling to formally inform their Korean customers tomorrow (the 23rd)."

The materials in short supply are Propylene Glycol Methyl Ether (PGME) and Propylene Glycol Methyl Ether Acetate (PGMEA). PGME and PGMEA are used as solvents in various electronic materials. A solvent is a liquid or gaseous substance used to dissolve other substances. Dissolution refers to the phenomenon in which one substance dissolves and mixes into another.

Semiconductor materials that use PGME and PGMEA include PR, Thinner, Bottom Anti-Reflective Coating (BARC), Spin-On-Hardmask (SOH), and temporary bonding adhesives for High Bandwidth Memory (HBM). This covers almost all photo patterning process materials. An industry source described the situation as, "It's like not being able to add water to instant coffee mix."

The Japanese companies supplying these materials to Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are numerous, including Shin-Etsu Chemical, Tokyo Ohka Kogyo (TOK), JSR, Fujifilm, and Nissan Chemical.

The reason for the PGME and PGMEA shortage is the Iran war. Japan depends on the Middle East for more than approximately 40% of its naphtha. When the Strait of Hormuz was effectively blockaded in early March, Middle Eastern naphtha supply was cut off. Naphtha is a light oil produced during crude oil refining. When decomposed at high temperatures, it yields basic petrochemical feedstocks such as propylene and ethylene. As a result, 6 of Japan's 12 naphtha cracking centers (NCCs) have entered production cuts. With propylene supply declining, the production of Propylene Oxide (PO)—which uses propylene as a feedstock—was hit. PGME and PGMEA, which use PO as a feedstock, have consequently faced production disruptions in a chain reaction. The spot price of Japanese naphtha jumped approximately 92%, from the USD 600s per ton before the blockade to USD 1,190 in early April.

Japan sources most of the raw materials for its semiconductor photo materials domestically. Japan's Daicel produces everything from PO to PGMEA in an integrated manner. Toagosei receives raw materials supplied by Dow and refines them into PGMEA, which it mass-produces. The PGME and PGMEA produced in this way are then received by domestic manufacturers such as JSR, TOK, Shin-Etsu Chemical, and Fujifilm, which turn them into finished products like PR for export to Korea.

An industry source pointed out, "Japan has a strong tendency to produce finished products using Japanese-made raw materials whenever possible," adding, "This self-sufficient structure is a strength in normal times, but when one raw material source is blocked like this, the entire chain shakes simultaneously."

Japanese photo material manufacturers are expected to review sourcing Korean or Chinese PGME and PGMEA. The key issue is the Process Change Notification (PCN) procedure. If the raw material for photo materials changes, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix must redo evaluations. This typically takes around one year. For leading-edge processes, it takes even longer.

Another source analyzed, "Thinner and SOH have been partially localized, but if Japanese supply of PR or BARC is cut off, semiconductor fabs could come to a halt," adding, "If there are major disruptions in material sourcing, some evaluation steps will inevitably have to be skipped."

Reflective benefits for the Korean industry are also expected. Chemtronics and Jaewon Industrial have already built PGMEA mass-production systems and are directly supplying the material to Japanese material companies and Samsung Electronics. An executive at Jaewon Industrial said, "The Korean industry has diversified raw material supply chains across the U.S. and China, so we are better off than Japan, but sourcing is not easy for us either—it's essentially the same situation."

Hanwul Soje Science plans to bring in PGME and PGMEA produced locally through its subsidiary JK Materials, which has signed an agreement with a major Chinese materials company referred to as "Company E." It is currently in supply discussions with a major Japanese photo material company on these items.

8-inch Foundry Prices on the Rise… Korean Foundries to See Full Benefit from Q2

The 8-inch foundry industry is enjoying a boom driven by rising power semiconductor demand and constrained production capacity.

On the 22nd, it was learned that DB HiTek plans to raise its 8-inch foundry process pricing by a single-digit percentage per wafer starting in Q2 of this year.

8-inch foundry refers to processes using wafers with a 200mm (millimeter) diameter. It is primarily used for mature (legacy) processes at 130 nanometers (nm) and above. The 8-inch foundry market began its full-fledged rebound last year. Power semiconductor demand has been rising across industries, while major players such as Samsung Electronics and TSMC have been gradually scaling down their 8-inch production capacity since last year.

Samsung Electronics is planning to completely shut down its Giheung 6-2 line, which produces 8-inch foundry output. An industry source explained, "Samsung Electronics is first clearing out products with poor profitability in 8-inch foundry," adding that "the related ecosystem is already within the sphere of influence."

As the 8-inch supply crunch intensifies, 8-inch foundries are also facing pricing pressure. China's SMIC already sent a notice to customers late last year informing them of a 10% price increase for its 8-inch BCD process. BCD is a power semiconductor process that implements three different power devices (Bipolar, CMOS, and DMOS) on a single chip, enhancing durability and power efficiency.

DB HiTek also mass-produces 8-inch BCD processes as its mainstay. It has been in continuous discussions with customers regarding process price increases. The price hike could be reflected as early as Q2 of this year, with the increase understood to be in the 3–5% range.

Utilization rates at the Bucheon and Sangwoo campuses are also high at over 90%. According to DB HiTek's Q1 business report, the company's average utilization rate stands at 91.96%.

An industry source stated, "Because there are various 8-inch processes, the situation differs slightly from case to case, but price increase discussions have been progressing steadily since late last year," and added, "As customers continue their inventory build-up stance, high utilization rates are expected to be maintained throughout this year."

[Exclusive] Samsung Scraps 7th-Generation DRAM Mass Production Plan… Red Flag for Future HBM Leadership

Samsung Electronics has scrapped its mass production plan for its 10nm-class 7th-generation DRAM (1d DRAM, hereafter D1d). Although the company had initially planned to begin actual D1d production after going through the Production Release Approval (PRA) process in Q1 of this year, it is understood that Samsung did not proceed with mass production after considering the deterioration in Return on Investment (ROI) stemming from the failure to meet yield targets.

According to a source familiar with Samsung Electronics' internal affairs on the 22nd, Samsung's management recently reviewed the yield and ROI of D1d and concluded that mass production was not viable. With process difficulty rising exponentially and stable product quality difficult to guarantee, management determined not to force line operations.

D1d is a core product that Samsung plans to apply to HBM5E, the 9th-generation High Bandwidth Memory. While 1c DRAM can handle the 6th through 8th generations (HBM4, HBM4E, HBM5), stable supply of D1d is essential starting from HBM5E.

This mass production cancellation raises the possibility of partial delays in Samsung Electronics' next-generation artificial intelligence (AI) memory roadmap. Previously, at GTC 2026 which opened on March 16 (local time) in San Jose, California, Samsung Electronics Memory Development VP Hwang Sang-joon stated, "D1d will be used as the core DRAM for HBM5E." The decision contradicts Hwang's presentation at the time, in which he expressed confidence in leveraging leading-edge processes.

Given the nature of the semiconductor business, a 1% difference in process yield is an indicator that determines trillions of won in operating profit. Samsung Electronics' current D1d appears to lack sufficient customer demand for the raw product to justify recouping the massive investment.

A source familiar with Samsung's internal affairs explained, "Along with the yield shortfall, management made the cold assessment that there are no customers willing to take or wait for D1d products at the current level." The judgment is that forcing mass production could lead to company-wide ROI deterioration.

With the mass production plan falling through, the approximately 400-person D1d mass production Task Force (TF) assembled for the project has effectively been left idle. The D1d mass production TF has been operating with mass production in mind for the past two years, but with the development product acceptance approval failing to come through, key engineers are reportedly confined to merely exchanging information at the development stage.

Inside Samsung Electronics, concerns over the DRAM technology gap with rival SK Hynix have reignited. SK Hynix is understood to have already completed D1d development and secured stable mass production yields of over 50%. Industry observers note that Samsung's strategy last year of simultaneously developing 6th-generation (1c) and 7th-generation (1d) DRAM dispersed its capabilities, leaving it at risk of falling behind rivals that relatively concentrated their firepower on a single generation.

A source familiar with Samsung's internal affairs said, "Samsung Electronics plans to indefinitely postpone the mass production schedule until D1d yields reach target levels, and as of now has not confirmed a timeline for resumption," adding, "The company is comprehensively re-examining its process roadmap and focusing on further boosting yields."

Samsung Electronics' China NAND Fab in "Transition Phase" as Equipment Swap Continues... "Production Losses to Extend into Next Year"

Samsung Electronics is undergoing equipment replacement and upgrades at its Xi'an NAND flash fab in China, and observers are now suggesting that the resulting production disruption will extend into next year. The Xi'an fab has historically had a relatively high share of legacy-node products such as 128-layer NAND. As mainstream products in the global NAND industry have moved up into the 200–300 layer range, the fab has been seen as showing its limits in terms of productivity and cost competitiveness.

Accordingly, Samsung Electronics has been carrying out line-wide upgrade work at the Xi'an fab since last year. However, analysts note that a temporary decline in NAND output is difficult to avoid during the process of removing existing tools, bringing in and installing new equipment, and then re-stabilizing the processes. While NAND profitability should improve, there is also a possibility that market share could shrink or plateau.

According to industry sources on the 22nd, Samsung Electronics' Xi'an fab's average monthly NAND wafer output has reportedly declined year-over-year. The industry estimates that production scale — which had stood at around 150K wafers per month — has been cut by roughly 5–6% this year. At a time when the global NAND market is widely seen as entering an upcycle, supply from the Xi'an fab — one of Samsung's key overseas production hubs — is moving in the opposite direction. This contrasts with competitors Japan's Kioxia and China's YMTC, both of which are gradually expanding capacity.

The industry points to the Xi'an fab's "transition phase" as the key reason for this production decline. Because NAND is built by stacking cells vertically to increase capacity, higher layer counts allow more data to be stored within the same area. Higher layer counts are therefore critical in terms of cost and productivity. However, the Xi'an fab has maintained a high share of 128-layer products for some time, fueling concerns that it could fall behind in the high-layer NAND race. The prevailing interpretation is that Samsung Electronics is accelerating equipment replacement — even at the cost of near-term production disruption — in order to secure medium- to long-term competitiveness.

In particular, competition has intensified as YMTC, China's largest NAND maker, has moved into mass production of products up to 294 layers. It has become difficult to hold off the Chinese challenge with 100-layer-range products, and in the commodity segment, pricing pressure is also increasing. From Samsung's standpoint, rather than maintaining volumes on existing processes, the company is now in a position where it needs to upgrade its lines and lift the mix of next-generation products. An additional variable is the possibility that bringing advanced equipment into China could become even more difficult if U.S. semiconductor restrictions on China are tightened further. A likely factor behind the decision is the judgment that major line upgrades need to be pulled forward as much as possible before the regulatory environment becomes more restrictive.

A full-scale semiconductor line upgrade is not something that ends simply by installing new tools. Even after the equipment swap, time is required to re-tune process conditions, stabilize yields, and re-align the product mix with market demand. The industry views large-scale equipment replacement at a memory fab as a long-haul project taking at least six months and, in some cases, more than a year. A semiconductor industry source explained: "Including yield, cycle time, and product mix, it's a reasonable estimate that the industry's perceived timing for full normalization is typically 6–9 months, and in some cases 12 months or more."

The NAND industry has faced supply disruptions during major process transitions in the past as well. When the industry shifted from planar NAND to 3D NAND, major players including Samsung Electronics and Kioxia all moved to swap out equipment at the same time, leading to a period of tight supply across the market. This is why there is a view that the Xi'an fab upgrade could affect future NAND market supply-demand dynamics and pricing — beyond being just a Samsung-specific issue. The industry's read is that Samsung Electronics will need to complete the shift of its production base toward next-generation NAND, even if that means absorbing short-term production losses, in order to defend its market leadership going forward.

[Exclusive] Samsung Electro-Mechanics to Supply AI Substrates to Broadcom

Riding the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, not only memory semiconductor companies but also Korean electronic component makers have moved to the center of the global materials, parts, and equipment (MPE) supply chain. Major players including Samsung Electro-Mechanics and LG Innotek have emerged as key partners for Big Tech firms seeking to resolve AI bottlenecks. Analysts say an era of "component-supplier supremacy" has arrived, with Korean companies now holding the upper hand in the supply chain — a reversal from the past subcontractor-style structure in which they relied on orders from finished-goods makers. 

According to industry sources on the 21st, Samsung Electro-Mechanics has secured Broadcom of the U.S. as a new customer for Flip Chip Ball Grid Array (FC-BGA) AI semiconductor substrates. Following major Big Tech names such as NVIDIA, Google, Amazon, and Apple, Broadcom has now joined Samsung Electro-Mechanics' customer roster. Samsung Electro-Mechanics will begin supplying substrates for Broadcom's most advanced AI accelerators starting in the second half of this year.

FC-BGA is a core component that connects semiconductor chips to the mainboard, transmitting electrical signals and power. Only a handful of companies are capable of manufacturing these substrates — Samsung Electro-Mechanics, LG Innotek, and Japan's Ibiden and Murata among them.

A tectonic shift is also underway in the Multi-Layer Ceramic Capacitor (MLCC) market. Samsung Electro-Mechanics is supplying large volumes of ultra-high-capacitance MLCCs for AI servers to NVIDIA and other major global Big Tech firms. AI servers use three to four times more MLCCs than conventional servers. In particular, these components must withstand high-temperature, high-pressure environments, requiring advanced technical capabilities, and unit prices run three to five times higher than standard products. This is why Samsung Electro-Mechanics and other Korean companies with specialized technologies, such as Amotech, are being courted by Big Tech.

There is also a growing view that the global AI supply chain is being restructured in such a way that it can no longer be sustained without Korean component makers. This is because Korean firms possess unrivaled technological capabilities in addressing the critical bottlenecks that determine the performance of AI accelerators.

An industry official said, "Korean companies have demonstrated irreplaceable technological capabilities in high-performance substrates and materials, and are now facing an unprecedented golden window of opportunity."

[EXCLUSIVE] Samsung Electronics to Build New Semiconductor Fab the Size of "4 Soccer Fields" in Onyang... To Become Core Back-end Process Hub

Samsung Electronics is restructuring the battleground of its HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) competition back toward the back-end process. The company is firming up plans to construct a new semiconductor fab of up to 8 stories and 8,870 pyeong at its Onyang campus in South Chungcheong Province, and to build out back-end process lines and packaging lines within it. The move is being read as a strategy to elevate Onyang—previously test-centric—into a comprehensive back-end hub for HBM, securing yield, delivery timelines, and customer responsiveness in one stroke.

According to industry sources on the 21st, Samsung Electronics is pushing ahead with plans to build a dedicated back-end fab on a new site within the Onyang campus. The building is planned at a minimum of 4 stories and up to 8 stories, and will house back-end process lines centered on a WP line, along with packaging lines. Analysts interpret this as evidence that discussions to expand HBM back-end functions at Onyang have moved beyond simple review into concrete equipment configuration.

◇ The scale itself is different... Onyang is not a mere supplement, but a back-end hub

What stands out first in this investment is the scale. 8,870 pyeong equates to roughly 29,326 ㎡—equivalent to placing approximately 349 units of 84㎡ apartments side by side. By international soccer field standards, the area exceeds about 4 fields. This is why the investment is being assessed not as a simple line reinforcement or auxiliary-building addition, but as the establishment of an independent back-end production axis for HBM response.

In the HBM market, there is a strong view that back-end operational capabilities—packaging, testing, logistics, and quality response—determine supply competitiveness just as much as front-end processes. Securing a large-scale back-end hub is thus read not as mere capacity expansion but as a strategic investment that shapes market responsiveness and customer trust.

Onyang has historically been evaluated as a site where testing and general packaging account for a relatively large share. By contrast, Cheonan has been the central axis for advanced packaging. If this investment materializes, Onyang is likely to emerge as a core back-end hub that goes beyond being a simple test site, executing HBM-grade packaging as well.

◇ Bringing testing and packaging under one roof

The core of this fab lies in its process configuration. Samsung Electronics is said to be moving toward building back-end process lines centered on the WP line together with PKG (packaging) lines. The WP line is a testing process that checks electrical characteristics and defects of chips at the wafer state, while PKG is the stage that stacks and packages the chips into finished products.

Integrating the two functions in a single space enables test results to be directly fed back into packaging, simultaneously boosting production efficiency and speed of quality response. Industry observers note that such an integrated operational structure becomes even more critical for products like HBM, where stacking structure, thermal control, and packaging precision dictate performance and yield.

Ultimately, this investment is interpreted less as a simple increase in equipment count and more as an effort to organically link testing and packaging to raise overall back-end operational efficiency. The industry sees the HBM market as having entered a phase where how stably you can package and how punctually you can supply matters more than how many you can make.

◇ Cheonan saturated, Onyang expanding... Full-scale shift in the HBM back-end axis

Behind Samsung Electronics' decision to play the Onyang expansion card lies the physical limits of Cheonan. The industry view is that the Cheonan campus already has little spatial slack, and the burden of retrofits—removing existing equipment to install new tools—is not insignificant either. To reliably support additional HBM demand, securing separate space is ultimately necessary, and Onyang expansion has emerged as the most realistic alternative.

If this investment is realized, the center of gravity of Samsung's back-end operations could shift. As advanced packaging functions that had been centered in Cheonan are dispersed to Onyang, the trend of Samsung's semiconductor production system broadening its stage—from front-end-centric competition to back-end operational competition—is likely to accelerate in earnest.

An industry official said, "In the AI semiconductor era, packaging has emerged as a variable that jointly determines both performance and supply," adding, "If the Onyang fab materializes as planned, Samsung Electronics' HBM gambit looks increasingly likely to be decided in the back-end, not the front-end."

text:
CXMT Struggles with HBM3 Development... Delay to H2 Likely

China's ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) is increasingly likely to push back the commercialization timeline for its 4th-generation high-bandwidth memory (HBM3). The company had initially targeted commercialization in the first half of this year, but it has yet to place mass-production-level orders with relevant materials and component suppliers.

According to industry sources on the 20th, CXMT is experiencing setbacks in its HBM3 mass production schedule, which had originally been targeted for the first half of this year.

CXMT is China's largest DRAM manufacturer. While its share of the global DRAM market remains outside the top tier, the company has been credited with rapidly advancing its technology, having successfully commercialized the latest DRAM standards including DDR5 and LPDDR5X.

CXMT is also knocking on the door of the HBM market—high-performance DRAM used in AI data centers. HBM is a memory semiconductor in which multiple DRAM dies are stacked vertically and connected through Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs). It requires highly advanced technology in both front-end and back-end processes.

The product CXMT is focused on developing is HBM3, a 4th-generation HBM that falls within the relatively mature (legacy) process category. Major players such as Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and Micron are ramping up full-scale mass production of HBM4 this year.

However, industry assessments indicate that CXMT's HBM3 remains at the testing stage. Although mass production had initially been targeted for as early as the first half of this year, the schedule has continued to slip. Orders for the materials and components required for HBM3 are reportedly still at the sample production level.

A semiconductor industry source explained, "CXMT's technological progress has been rapid, but the HBM3 mass production schedule keeps being pushed back. Judging from development progress, mass production within this year appears unlikely."

Meanwhile, CXMT has adopted G4 (16nm-class) DRAM as the core die for its HBM3. This is the DRAM node for which full-scale mass production began last year, representing CXMT's most advanced process.

For the back-end process of stacking DRAM dies, CXMT has adopted Mass Reflow-Molded Underfill (MR-MUF).

MR-MUF is a technology that temporarily bonds each DRAM die with heat as it is stacked, then finalizes the bonding by applying heat (reflow) once the full stack is complete. Liquid EMC (Epoxy Molding Compound—a molding material blending epoxy polymer with inorganic silica) is then applied. Currently, SK Hynix utilizes the MR-MUF process.

[EXCLUSIVE] Qualcomm CEO Visits Korea, Meets with Samsung Foundry Leadership… Memory Cooperation Talks with SK

Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon visited Korea on the 21st for back-to-back meetings with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix executives. The visit is seen as an effort to concretize cooperation on the cutting-edge 2nm (nanometer; 1nm = one billionth of a meter) foundry process and to address memory supply-demand tightness that has intensified with the spread of artificial intelligence (AI).

Amon met exclusively with The Korea Economic Daily at a hotel in Banpo-dong, Seoul, earlier that day. Having entered the country via Gimpo Airport the previous day, he is carrying out his Korea trip schedule through today. Dressed in a blue shirt and tie, Amon exited the hotel without responding to reporters' questions.

The central agenda of Amon's visit is cooperation with Samsung Foundry. On this day, Amon is meeting with Samsung Electronics Foundry Business Division President Han Jin-man and other foundry executives. The two sides are expected to discuss producing Qualcomm's next-generation application processor (AP), the Snapdragon 8 Elite 2, on Samsung Electronics' 2nm process (SF2). At CES 2026 in January, Amon stated, "We have begun discussions with Samsung Electronics on utilizing the 2nm process for foundry production, and design work has been completed."

If a contract is signed, it would mark the return of Qualcomm's cutting-edge volume to Samsung after five years, having shifted to TSMC in 2022. Industry analysts attribute Qualcomm's renewed interest in Samsung Foundry to the latter having restored technological credibility by resolving its chronic yield and thermal issues. Samsung Electronics' July 2024 win of a $16.5 billion (approx. KRW 24 trillion) order from Tesla for production of the next-generation AI chip AI6 also contributed to the improved perception of its technological capabilities. Analysts also view the move as a strategic diversification, as TSMC's wafer prices continue to rise, pushing Qualcomm to dual-source next-generation chip production through Samsung to reduce dependency.

Amon also met with SK Hynix executives to discuss memory semiconductor supply-demand arrangements. With the recent expansion of the AI server and on-device AI markets intensifying shortages in core memory products such as LPDDR (low-power) DRAM, Qualcomm has moved to secure allocations directly. As Qualcomm pushes into the server market in earnest with its AI accelerator "AI200," unveiled last year, cooperation on High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) and SOCAMM is also understood to have been discussed in depth. The move mirrors recent Korea visits by the CEOs of Nvidia and AMD, who similarly reinforced memory partnerships.

An industry official commented, "Qualcomm has effectively re-evaluated Samsung Foundry's technological capabilities and acknowledged SK's influence in memory. It was an occasion that once again confirmed the standing of Korean companies in the global semiconductor supply chain."

Separately, it is understood that Amon did not meet with Samsung Electronics DX Division President Roh Tae-moon — a key customer of Qualcomm's Snapdragon series — during this trip.

urls.description: TrendForce’s latest research indicates that the global market for AI-focused optical transceivers has entered a phase of rapid growth, with market size projected to expand from US$16.5 billion in 2025 to $26 billion in 2026, representing over 57% YoY growth. This surge is driven not only by specification upgrades but also reflects a broader structural reshaping of the optical communications supply chain amid accelerating AI data center deployment.

text:
▶ Global AI Optical Transceiver Market to Reach US$26 Billion in 2026; Component Shortages Identified as Primary Capacity Expansion Bottleneck — TrendForce

• TrendForce expects the global AI optical transceiver market to expand from US$16.5 billion in 2025 to US$26 billion in 2026, representing 57% YoY growth.

• This acceleration reflects not only specification upgrades but also a structural reshaping of the optical communications supply chain, driven by the faster pace of AI data center buildouts.

• As AI data center expansion continues, demand for 800G-and-above optical transceivers — used for interconnects between AI server clusters — is surging.

• North American CSP data center traffic is sustaining annual growth of over 30%, with aggressive GPU and AI server deployments by major cloud players driving high growth in high-speed optical interconnects.

• However, constrained production capacity for core optoelectronic chips such as EMLs and CW-LDs is deepening supply shortages, acting as the primary bottleneck for overall optical transceiver capacity expansion.

• In addition, high-precision manufacturing processes such as optical alignment are difficult to scale, and the pace of productivity improvement faces structural limits.

• At the same time, the rising power consumption and heat dissipation challenges of high-speed optical modules are increasing system design complexity, adding pressure on actual data center deployment and mass-production schedules.

• Upstream suppliers, led by NVIDIA and key system vendors, are shifting their procurement strategies — adopting strategic long-term agreements (LTAs) to secure critical components and reduce dependence on short-term spot-market purchases, thereby mitigating supply risk.

• TrendForce emphasizes that growth in the AI optical transceiver market is shifting from a single-product upgrade narrative toward three axes: market expansion, generational technology transitions, and application diversification.

• As 1.6T-generation products gradually enter mass production, demand for edge computing and data center interconnect (DCI) applications is expected to rise, fueling growth in the 800G and 1.6T ZR/ZR+ coherent optical module market.

• In response to component shortages, major international players such as Coherent, Lumentum, and AAOI — along with Taiwanese firms including ELASER and LuxNet Corporation — are moving to expand capacity and adopt new technologies.

• 2026–2027 will be a critical window for establishing positions in the 1.6T supply chain, with success in design-ins at tier-1 customers expected to be the decisive factor for future market share.

UMC Reportedly Approached for 2D NAND Foundry Work, But Faces Three Major Hurdles: People, Technology, and Equipment

With international memory manufacturers' exit from 2D NAND flash memory now all but confirmed, supply scarcity has driven a sharp surge in low-density 2D NAND prices. Recent market chatter suggests that UMC (聯電) may receive SLC/MLC Flash foundry orders, raising the prospect that the future oligopolistic supply structure of 2D NAND could be broken.

However, according to industry sources speaking to DIGITIMES, while flash memory foundry opportunities have indeed been discussed with UMC over the past several months, the absence of three core elements — manpower, process integration and development capability, and equipment — has emerged as the most significant obstacle.

NAND Flash Prices Rising Faster Than DRAM

According to supply chain sources, NAND Flash prices have climbed sharply since the start of 2026, with the rate of increase already outpacing DRAM. The supply shortfall is particularly severe for MLC NAND and SLC NAND, where prices for legacy-process low-density products have surged nearly 10-fold. Downstream players report that MLC NAND prices were raised by roughly 30% in April.

Regarding the market rumor that Asian customers have approached UMC about flash memory foundry orders, the industry generally views the current strength in MLC/SLC NAND prices as potentially more attractive in profitability terms than mature logic processes.

That said, existing equipment cannot be used directly, and retrofitting lines or purchasing new tools would take an estimated 1–2 years. Given the enormous scale of the current 2D NAND supply shortage, this would do little to ease the supply gap.

Moreover, the bottlenecks at the execution stage are far more complex than outsiders anticipate.

Hurdle ①: People — The 2D NAND Engineers Are Gone

Industry sources privately disclosed that, in an effort to resolve the MLC/SLC NAND supply crunch, internal proposals were made to explore the feasibility of flash memory foundry work at UMC. However, formidable bottlenecks exist across multiple dimensions — talent, technology, and equipment.

First, potential IP licensors and NAND manufacturers are not opposed to licensing partnerships in principle. The problem lies in the requirement that support must come from manufacturers with actual mass-production experience, including dispatching technical teams to help implement the process.

The issue is that engineers who once tuned 2D NAND equipment have largely retired or moved on, and those who remain have been redeployed to 3D NAND mass-production roles. At present, NAND manufacturers are concentrating their resources on 3D NAND R&D to capture growth opportunities from AI server applications. With manpower stretched thin, they simply cannot afford to take on additional 2D NAND technical support.

Hurdle ②: Technology — UMC's Memory Development Capability Gap

Second, while UMC did conduct memory-related R&D years ago and currently has some idle fab space that could accommodate foundry orders, its core technology has drifted significantly from the memory domain. Re-entry would require enormous resource investment, and rebuilding process fine-tuning and yield optimization capabilities would take considerable time.

If UMC can only provide production capacity without the underlying technology, it would be unable to support customers through process development and integration on its own — leaving the realistic profit contribution to UMC quite limited.

Hurdle ③: Equipment — No Path to Securing Legacy Tools

Third, the equipment problem has no ready solution. International manufacturers' legacy tools have already been sold off or dismantled during line upgrades, and even if used equipment could be located, related maintenance parts and personnel would be hard to secure.

Previously, Japanese giant Kioxia also told DIGITIMES that the discontinuation of legacy products such as 2D NAND was not driven by AI-related capacity crowd-out, but rather by the extremely high cost of maintaining legacy equipment and issues related to equipment aging.

That said, if UMC were to take on flash memory foundry orders and rebuild via new equipment purchases, the implementation process and yields would differ from the legacy approach, likely requiring fresh trial-and-error and development. This implies considerable uncertainty around investment recovery. Additionally, the IC design houses involved are unfamiliar with actual foundry process and mass-production realities — and while their appetite for collaboration is strong, on balance, the idea of a foundry arrangement via technology transfer currently lacks any viable near-term solution.

UMC Notifies Customers of Price Hikes Effective H2 2026

UMC's official spokesperson declined to comment on market rumors regarding flash memory foundry work. However, the company has recently issued price-increase notices to customers and partners, confirming pricing hikes for the second half of 2026.

UMC stated that since the first half of 2026, it has observed robust demand resilience across diverse application areas including communications, industrial, consumer electronics, and AI-related segments. Combined with rising costs across key drivers such as raw materials, energy, and logistics, the company will implement wafer price adjustments in the second half of 2026.

According to related supply chain players, UMC is raising prices across both 8-inch and 12-inch product lines. Based on a roughly 3.5-month cycle, orders taped out in April are expected to be subject to the new pricing.

- 8-inch wafer lines: relatively higher increases of around 10–15%
- 12-inch lines (80nm, 55nm, 40nm, etc.): increases of roughly 5–10%

Adjustments will be tiered based on individual customer volumes. This round of price hikes is primarily aimed at recovering prior price cuts on mature processes. Since some IC players have locked in long-term agreements (LTAs), the impact will be limited, and the increases are expected to be gradually passed through to downstream customers over time.

text:
ASMPT Secures Multiple HBM4 TC Bonder Orders Last Year... SK Hynix Likely Among Buyers

Singapore-headquartered ASMPT appears to have secured orders for 6th-generation High Bandwidth Memory (HBM4) Thermal Compression (TC) bonders from memory companies including SK Hynix.

At its 2025 earnings conference call, ASMPT stated: "We were the first to secure TC bonder equipment orders for 12-high HBM4 from multiple customers," adding that "through Q4 shipments last year, we established meaningful share in the memory market." HBM4 has currently been commercialized up to 12-high.

Founded in Hong Kong in 1975, ASMPT is a semiconductor packaging (back-end) equipment supplier now headquartered in Singapore, with production hubs in Huizhou and Shenzhen (China), Shanghai, and Singapore.

TC bonders are core equipment that stack semiconductor chips using heat and pressure. This process is currently applied to HBM up to 12-high. However, as the industry moves to 20-high and beyond, hybrid bonding is emerging as an alternative. Hybrid bonding directly joins copper-to-copper (Cu-Cu) without using "bumps" (solder protrusions) between chips.

CEO Robin Ng noted, "HBM CAPEX moves in the same direction as data center investment," adding, "as we progress from 12-high to 16-high and 20-high, TC bonder demand will also expand." He continued, "TC bonding can address up to 16-high, but at 20-high, hybrid bonding may be partially adopted in accordance with JEDEC standards."

ASMPT is currently developing equipment for 16-high applications. Its flux-based tools are at the sampling stage, while fluxless process tools are at customer qualification. Hybrid bonder shipments are expanding following customer approval, and a 2nd-generation tool is also under development.

TC Bonder Revenue Surges 146%... Samsung Also Reportedly Evaluating Equipment

TC bonders drove the earnings performance. ASMPT posted full-year revenue of HKD 13.7362 billion (approximately KRW 2.57 trillion) and operating profit of HKD 625.5 million (approximately KRW 110 billion), representing year-on-year growth of 10% and 8.8%, respectively.

TC bonder revenue surged 146% over the same period. ASMPT stated, "Through entry into the HBM market, we significantly raised our TC bonder share," explaining that "last year's share gain reflected the impact of large orders secured in Q4 2024."

When asked on the call whether its current share stood at around 30%, the company responded, "within that range." However, this may be interpreted as referring to the entire TC bonder market including both logic and HBM applications. ASMPT has set a target of 35–40% share in the expanded TCB market by 2028. In the HBM-dedicated TC bonder market, Hanmi Semiconductor ranks first with 71.2% share.

Order momentum is also continuing. The company explained, "This year marks the emergence of new demand for 16-high-capable TC bonders," adding that "additional orders will depend on customers' 16-high mass production pace and the launch schedule of (NVIDIA's) next-generation GPU architecture."

ASMPT further stated, "We expect Q1 orders this year to increase approximately 20% QoQ and approximately 40% YoY," noting that "this could mark the highest quarterly order level in the past four years."

Meanwhile, Samsung Electronics is reportedly evaluating the adoption of ASMPT equipment alongside Netherlands-based BESI, the global No. 1 in hybrid bonders.

"TC Bonder Market to Reach USD 1.6 Billion"... Hanmi-Hanwha Competition Seen as Tailwind

The market itself is expanding. ASMPT projects the total TC bonder market to grow from USD 759 million (approximately KRW 1.114 trillion) last year to USD 1.6 billion (approximately KRW 2.3484 trillion) by 2028, implying a CAGR of approximately 30%.

Hanmi Semiconductor plans to launch a prototype of its 2nd-generation hybrid bonder within the year. It is constructing a dedicated "Hybrid Bonder Factory" in Juan, Incheon, with an investment of approximately KRW 100 billion, targeting operational start in the first half of next year.

Late entrant Hanwha Semitech recently supplied a 2nd-generation hybrid bonder prototype to SK Hynix, which is now set to undergo performance validation testing. This comes approximately four years after its 1st-generation equipment delivery in 2022.

Samsung Electronics' semiconductor equipment affiliate SEMES and LG Electronics' Production Engineering Research Institute are also reportedly developing hybrid bonders.

Separately, some industry observers view the patent dispute between Hanmi Semiconductor and Hanwha Semitech as a potential tailwind for ASMPT. With the two companies engaged in mutual litigation over TC bonder architecture and flux process technology, customers are increasingly likely to pursue equipment dual-sourcing and evaluate new suppliers.

Another variable is SK Hynix's consideration of hybrid bonder adoption for HBM5 (8th generation) to be deployed in 2029.
