text:
[Exclusive] Samsung Foundry 2nm Yield at 55%… Stuck Below the 'Mass Production 60%' Threshold

Samsung Electronics' foundry business — a key future growth engine — has hit a wall at the '60% mass production' threshold for its 2nm (nanometer; 1nm = one-billionth of a meter) process. With yields stuck in the mid-50% range and failing to enter stable mass production territory, effective yields are expected to drop to the 40% range once back-end processing is factored in. While the company has succeeded in achieving technical entry, the consensus is that it remains insufficient to win orders from global Big Tech clients.

According to semiconductor industry sources on the 13th, Samsung Electronics' foundry division's average yield for the 2nm process is understood to be approximately 55%. This is lower than the '60%-plus' estimates floated by some, signaling that additional time is still needed to reach mass production stability. A source with knowledge of internal affairs stated, "The 2nm process yield is in the 50–60% range, with an average around 55%," adding, "The process is running, but it is still a long way from a stable mass production phase."

The pace of yield improvement itself has been rapid. Samsung's foundry 2nm yields were reportedly stuck in the 20% range as recently as the second half of last year. Reaching the mid-50s in less than a year is assessed as technically reaching a level where the mass production line can be operated. This is attributed in part to the accumulation of process experience driven by incoming orders for Bitcoin mining chips from China's Canaan and MicroBT, among others. Given the extreme difficulty of the 2nm ultra-fine process, some consider this an exceptionally fast rate of improvement.

However, the prevailing view in the industry is that it remains a "half-process" at best. In a structure where nearly half of all wafer input is discarded as defective, the process fails on both price competitiveness and delivery reliability. In particular, when factoring in losses from performance binning and packaging, the actual percentage of chips that can generate profit is estimated to fall as low as 40%. Considering that a single wafer for cutting-edge processes costs tens of millions of won, a 1% difference in yield translates to annual operating profit differences ranging from hundreds of billions to trillions of won. This is bound to significantly derail Samsung Electronics' efforts to improve foundry business profitability.

An industry source said, "A yield in the 50% range only means the process 'runs' — it is not a stage where customers can entrust orders with confidence," adding, "It is a zone where both delivery and quality variability coexist."

By contrast, rival TSMC is reported to have secured stable yields of 60–70% for its 2nm process. Samsung Foundry's current mid-50% yield is therefore assessed as corresponding to the technical entry stage, but falling short for securing major customers — a "transitional zone." Significant progress has been made, but analysis suggests actual mass production remains premature.

In practice, Samsung has secured some customer and internal volumes, but has yet to achieve results in winning key clients such as Apple, NVIDIA, and AMD. Notably, Qualcomm — a global mobile application processor (AP) company that had raised expectations for new orders — is also showing signs of returning to TSMC, citing process yield and stability concerns. Additionally, the 'AI6' advanced autonomous driving chip contracted with Tesla is scheduled for mass production this year, and the yield level achieved at the actual production milestone will be critical in determining profitability and supply stability.

Meanwhile, Samsung Electronics' strategy is to win new orders, run its facilities, and improve yields going forward. At Samsung Electronics' annual general meeting on March 18, Han Jin-man, head of the foundry business division (President), stated, "For the 2nm process as well (which is at a higher level than the 4nm process), we can build up order experience with major companies and secure yields through that process."

text:
NAND Stacking 'HBF' Process Market Opens… SanDisk Begins Building Supply Chain

The market for 'High Bandwidth Flash (HBF)' — a process that dramatically boosts performance and capacity by stacking NAND flash memory in a manner similar to High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) — has officially opened. This comes as SanDisk, which first unveiled HBF technology, has begun building out its materials, components, and equipment supply chain. With major memory manufacturers successively launching HBF development efforts, attention is turning to whether it will generate manufacturing demand on par with HBM.

According to industry sources on April 13, SanDisk has begun establishing an ecosystem with related supply chain partners to set up a pilot production line for HBF prototypes. The company plans to showcase prototypes in the second half of this year, and this is understood to involve the construction of a new pilot line. Japan is emerging as the leading candidate for the production site.

A senior supply chain industry executive said, "SanDisk is in discussions with materials and equipment companies, targeting major equipment installation in H2," adding that "some companies have already begun purchase order (PO) negotiations." The industry expects the pilot line buildout to be completed in H2 with operations commencing around year-end. Commercial production is targeted for next year.

HBF is a next-generation flash memory concept unveiled by SanDisk in February of last year. Its core architecture is similar to HBM. HBM, which has seen rapid growth recently as it underpins AI computation, achieves dramatically higher speed (bandwidth) and performance by stacking DRAM. HBF instead stacks NAND flash to increase not only bandwidth but also capacity. While HBM is a memory optimized for speed — real-time computation for AI training — HBF maximizes capacity. Unlike DRAM, NAND retains data without power (non-volatile), drawing attention as a new storage solution for AI.

As HBF production infrastructure buildout accelerates, demand for process-related materials, components, and equipment is also expected to expand — signaling the emergence of an entirely new process market for manufacturing an unprecedented product. With SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics also preparing HBF alongside SanDisk, the pace of market growth could accelerate. SK Hynix is collaborating with SanDisk on HBF standardization and other initiatives, while Samsung Electronics is independently gearing up to enter the market.

Professor Kim Jung-ho of KAIST, at an HBF technology roadmap presentation in February, projected that HBF could surpass HBM in market size by 2038.

The HBF process is expected to favor the existing supply chain ecosystem that has served HBM manufacturing, given the process similarities. Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs) are used to transmit signals between stacked NAND layers. text:
DRAM Price Growth Rate Expected to Slow from 70%+ in Q1 to 30–50% in Q2

Global DRAM price growth is forecast to decelerate from over 70% in Q1 to 30–50% in Q2, according to new projections. While DRAM supply shortages are expected to persist on an annual basis this year, demand softening may emerge in certain end applications.

Market research firm SigmaIntell recently stated, "DRAM prices will continue to rise in Q2, but the magnitude of increases will vary by product. DDR4 price increases will narrow significantly, while DDR5 and LPDDR5X still have room to rise." The firm projected that "the global average DRAM price increase will decelerate from over 70% in Q1 to the 30–50% range in Q2."

In H2 2026, DRAM price growth is expected to moderate further to 5–20%, with prices stabilizing at elevated levels by year-end. SigmaIntell cited the following factors: ▲stabilization of DRAM makers' capacity allocation, ▲gradual unwinding of urgent stockpiling demand from AI server and cloud service providers (CSPs), and ▲easing of panic buying. SigmaIntell added that "DRAM supply shortages should ease to some extent as consumer electronics and IT product demand softens."

Based on DDR and HBM capacity allocation trends and demand shifts, SigmaIntell projects the global DRAM supply-demand balance will swing from an 8% oversupply in 2025 to a 12% undersupply in 2026. The AI-driven DRAM supercycle, which began in H2 2025, is likely to continue this year.

AI server DRAM demand is expected to grow 105% YoY this year. By contrast, conventional server DRAM demand growth is projected at just 3% over the same period.

Consumer electronics and IT product DRAM demand is expected to decline YoY this year. Their share of total DRAM bit consumption is forecast to fall from 54% in 2025 to 42% in 2026. Demand declines may be particularly pronounced in budget PCs, low-end smartphones, and IoT devices.

SigmaIntell projects that HBM's share of global DRAM wafer capacity will exceed 20% this year. HBM is a dedicated memory for AI server GPUs. HBM bit demand is expected to grow 110% YoY this year. The expansion of HBM's share of DRAM wafer capacity — driven by factors such as the ramp of HBM4 mass production this year — could squeeze the capacity available for DDR products.

As of the end of Q1 2026, server DRAM contract prices had risen 3–4x compared to Q2 2025. Over the same period, DDR4 prices rose 4x and DDR5 prices rose 3.5x.

By comparison, consumer electronics and IT product DRAM prices rose later. These segments began experiencing DRAM supply shortages starting in Q4 2025. As of end-Q1, DDR contract prices in the consumer/IT segment were 2–2.5x higher than Q2 2025 levels.

SigmaIntell noted that consumer electronics and IT companies can no longer pursue all markets and product lineups, and will need to make strategic choices. Component price increases, including memory, have been passed through to finished product prices. End-product price hikes may suppress demand particularly for low-end products, potentially leading to an overall decline in consumer electronics and IT product demand.

Silicon Photonics Mass Production Hinges on Wafer Test Chain — 'Electrical-on-Top, Optical-on-Bottom' Architecture Is Key

As AI compute demand pushes high-speed transmission efficiency to its absolute limits, 2026 is widely regarded as the pivotal year for silicon photonics (SiPh) and co-packaged optics (CPO) to enter large-scale deployment — making it an urgent new battleground the industry is racing to stake out.

Notably, the success or failure of this silicon photonics mass production campaign now rests squarely on the shoulders of the semiconductor test supply chain.

According to OSAT industry sources, silicon photonics chip testing comprises three sequential process steps, and the most formidable production barrier currently lies at the wafer-level opto-electrical integrated test — referred to as the "electrical-on-top, optical-on-bottom" (上電下光) configuration. As this test sits at the second stage of the overall test insertion flow, the industry calls it "Insertion 2."

Specifically, because TSMC employs its SoIC technology to vertically stack the electronic IC (EIC) on top of the photonic IC (PIC), the resulting Compact Universal Photonic Engine (COUPE) must pass a dual-sided wafer test — electrical probing from the top, optical probing from the bottom — in order to screen known-good die from defective ones.

The core technical bottleneck is as follows: because the test conditions for optical and electrical signals differ significantly, no production-worthy automated test solution currently exists on the market.

For this reason, Insertion 2 has been dubbed a "black hole" in silicon photonics testing within the semiconductor industry — it is neither fast enough nor accurate enough.

In other words, how to develop a low-cost, high-efficiency automated test solution is intensely challenging the R&D capabilities of ATE (automated test equipment) vendors and test interface suppliers alike. If this bottleneck cannot be overcome to achieve economies of scale, it risks significantly dampening the market's willingness to adopt CPO in the near term.

Under mounting pressure from customers' production timelines, major test equipment players Advantest and Teradyne, along with leading test interface companies FormFactor, MPI Corporation (旺矽), and Hermes Testing (漢民測試), are accelerating the development of automated test solutions to clear the wafer-level opto-electrical integration hurdle and secure a first-mover position on this beachhead.

Additionally, supply chain sources note that the remaining two test steps for silicon photonics chips — "Insertion 1," corresponding to photonic IC testing, and "Insertion 3," corresponding to post-CPO-packaging final product testing — already have relatively mature automated solutions available on the market.

Regarding Insertion 1 product positioning, Advantest stated that "Triton," an integrated solution co-developed with FormFactor, is currently undergoing equipment qualification at customer sites and is expected to be formally deployed before year-end to support PIC testing in production.

For the critical mass production bottleneck at Insertion 2, the solution proposed by Advantest and its supply chain partners is expected to complete proof of concept (PoC) in the first half of the year, with the prospect of entering a joint development phase with customers in the second half.

Industry analysis indicates that silicon photonics chips face significantly elevated requirements for stability and accuracy in high-speed transmission environments, raising the overall test technology threshold in tandem. In particular, because the cost of detecting failures in silicon photonics chips after CPO packaging is completed is extremely high, Shift-Left Testing has become critically important — phased verification at earlier stages is now seen as the last line of defense for protecting margins.

However, supply chain sources revealed that if the electrical-on-top/optical-on-bottom test bottleneck fails to achieve an equipment-level breakthrough in a timely manner, test houses may opt to selectively skip Insertion 2 during initial mass production, betting instead on Insertion 3 where solutions are well-defined — a compromise that sacrifices some yield and cost efficiency in exchange for keeping final product shipment schedules on track.

SanDisk Secures Korean Materials/Parts/Equipment Allies, Accelerates HBF Development… Timeline Moved Up by Six Months

U.S. NAND flash maker SanDisk is accelerating the development of its next-generation product, High Bandwidth Flash (HBF). In the process, Korean semiconductor industry players are emerging as key allies.

SanDisk is pursuing collaboration on HBF sample production with materials, parts, and equipment (MPE) companies that possess unrivaled competitiveness in specific fields. If the HBF market grows going forward, the benefits are expected to extend to Korea's semiconductor industry as well. Whether Samsung Electronics and SK hynix will also pick up the pace on their own product development is drawing attention.

According to semiconductor industry sources on April 9, SanDisk has recently begun collaborating with select Korean semiconductor MPE companies on HBF sample fabrication. Industry sources indicate that a company with a monopoly on certain equipment used in High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) manufacturing is expected to ship sample equipment to SanDisk around early this summer.

HBF is one of the next-generation growth drivers attracting global memory semiconductor industry attention after HBM. While HBM is made by vertically stacking DRAM dies, HBF is made by stacking NAND. It is slower than HBM but offers the advantage of processing data with significantly larger capacity.

The prevailing view in the semiconductor industry is that HBF will be complementary to HBM rather than a substitute. Rather than cannibalizing each other, both markets are expected to expand. The industry projects the HBF market will begin growing in earnest around 2030.

Professor Kim Jung-ho of KAIST's Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering — often called the "Father of HBM" — stated at a February presentation on HBF technology development and commercialization strategy that "by 2038, the HBF market will be larger than the current HBM market."

According to SanDisk's website, on August 6 of last year (local time), the company partially revealed its future roadmap in a post titled "Beyond the Memory Wall: The Inside Story of SanDisk HBF for AI Inference." It projected HBF samples would ship in H2 of this year, with HBF-based AI device samples emerging in early 2027.

An industry source said, "As sample production ramps up in earnest, SanDisk appears set to pull its previously announced HBF development roadmap forward by roughly six months," adding, "This reflects the strength of SanDisk's determination to lead the market."

Industry observers note that SanDisk's push to accelerate HBF development is also influenced by its identity as a pure NAND flash company. Without HBM — which is made from DRAM — in its portfolio, the analysis is that SanDisk is going all-in on capturing this new market.

Among Korean memory semiconductor companies, SK hynix is the most proactive on HBF. SK hynix signed an MOU with SanDisk in August of last year to pursue HBF standardization. In February of this year, the company announced it held a kickoff event for an HBF spec standardization consortium at SanDisk's U.S. headquarters.

However, the SK hynix–SanDisk collaboration is focused on establishing HBF standards and has not yet progressed to the stage of joint mass production. Both companies are expected to develop and bring their own products to market independently.

SK hynix CEO Kwak Noh-jung stated at the company's annual general meeting on March 25, "We will proactively secure next-generation portfolios including Processing-in-Memory (PIM), Compute Express Link (CXL), and HBF, and leap forward as a 'Full-Stack AI Memory Creator' that proposes more than what customers want."

An SK hynix spokesperson said, "Beyond what was announced around February regarding HBF standardization efforts with SanDisk, we are unable to confirm specific details of the development roadmap."

Samsung Electronics has not publicly disclosed any HBF roadmap or development plans. However, according to industry sources, Samsung is also reportedly preparing for HBF development.

text:
Will Murata Fire the Opening Shot for MLCC Price Hikes?

The MLCC (Multi-Layer Ceramic Capacitor) market is rebounding on the back of expanding demand from AI servers and automotive components. The key question is whether Japan's Murata will signal a price increase at its earnings announcement later this month. While price hikes are seen as inevitable, the consensus is that broad-based increases will only materialize after Murata—the market leader—fires the first shot.

According to industry sources on April 12, Murata is expected to provide directional guidance on MLCC pricing policy at its earnings release on April 30 (local time). The industry expects Murata to review Q1 demand trends and then outline the scope and likelihood of price increases. An industry official said, "Once Murata delivers a pricing message at its earnings call, pricing policies across domestic and international MLCC players will begin to take shape."

Signs of shifting supply-demand dynamics are emerging in the MLCC market, particularly in high-value-added products. Lead times are extending for high-capacitance, high-voltage MLCCs used in AI servers and high-reliability products for automotive applications, with some models showing early signs of supply shortages. Companies are focusing on expanding their mix toward AI server and automotive products. As semiconductor performance improves, MLCC content per device increases, suggesting demand will remain solid for the time being.

However, the demand recovery has not immediately translated into price hikes. While prices for some passive components such as inductors and ferrites have adjusted, MLCC pricing moves have been limited. Industry observers note that a wait-and-see game is underway, with competitors waiting to gauge customer reactions after Murata moves on pricing before deciding whether to follow suit.

This caution is rooted in past experience. MLCCs faced severe supply shortages during the post-COVID IT demand surge in 2020–2021, driving sharp price increases—reportedly averaging around 23%. The situation reversed sharply in 2022 as global demand cooled rapidly. Inventories piled up, prices fell, and some commodity MLCCs reverted to pre-hike levels. Set makers pushed back hard, and component suppliers were forced to adjust utilization rates and endure margin compression.

A components industry executive who lived through that period explained, "COVID-era IT demand was front-loaded, creating a demand vacuum afterward. We experienced a sharp run-up followed by a steep decline." He added, "Since then, MLCC makers have adopted much more conservative pricing policies across the board." He continued, "Current demand is strong, but further price increases remain a delicate matter. The MLCC market has too many players to create a supercycle structure like semiconductors."

The MLCC market features competition among Japanese, Korean, and Taiwanese players. Even if one company raises prices preemptively, customers can switch suppliers if competitors don't follow. The high share of commodity products for smartphones, consumer electronics, and other applications is also a constraint—commodity products are highly sensitive to inventory levels and pricing, making broad-based price increases difficult.

MLCC pricing follows the No. 1 player. The prevailing industry view is that Murata will move first on pricing, after which competitors will follow once customer reactions are assessed.

There is no shortage of variables going forward. Tariffs, geopolitical risks, and elections in major economies could significantly swing end-market demand. The components industry's high dependency on set-maker demand is another overhang. An industry official noted, "Component companies are structurally dependent on growth in downstream industries. If the overall market expands, revenues can grow even if market share shifts somewhat."

Overall, the directional case for MLCC price increases remains intact, but the dominant view is that it is premature to expect a sharp upcycle like the past. Rather than an industry-wide blanket increase, the most realistic scenario is a gradual rise in ASPs (average selling prices) centered on high-value-added segments such as AI servers and automotive.

Another industry source said, "Price increases are a matter of time, but the pace will be gradual. For now, the market will remain in a phase of watching Murata's decision and customer reactions."

Bank of Korea: Today's AI Supercycle Through the Lens of Dot-Com Era Telecom Infrastructure Investment

In the late 1990s, during the dot-com bubble, telecom companies competitively invested in long-haul fiber optic cables, driven by expectations that internet and telecom demand would sustain high growth. At the time, the optimistic belief that "internet traffic doubles every three to four months" was widely held across the market, and this perception, combined with telecom operators' aggressive capacity expansion funded through external borrowing such as corporate bonds and loans, led to massive overinvestment in telecom infrastructure. [Figures 23, 24] Furthermore, major telecom equipment vendors including Cisco, Lucent, and Nortel widely offered vendor financing to new telecom operators, tying the financing to purchases of their own equipment. However, as actual demand growth fell short of expectations, unused capacity — known as dark fiber — accumulated, and investment contracted rapidly alongside plunging stock prices.

An interesting point is that technological progress at the time actually exacerbated the overcapacity problem. A prime example is wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM) technology, which enabled multiple wavelengths of signals to be transmitted simultaneously through a single optical fiber strand within a cable, dramatically expanding transmission capacity. As a result, not only was new fiber being laid, but the effective capacity of existing fiber optic cables was also increasing rapidly, causing supply capability to far exceed actual demand. [Figure 25] This case illustrates that even when initial demand generated by a new technology is very strong, competitive capacity buildouts based on rosy demand forecasts, combined with faster-than-expected technological innovation, can trigger a rapid shift to overcapacity in a given industry. That said, while the overinvestment of the era caused fiber optic cable prices to plunge and forced a painful adjustment across the sector, in hindsight, the telecom infrastructure and technological advances accumulated through this process served as the long-term foundation for the IT industry's subsequent development — a positive legacy worth acknowledging.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics to Build ‘MLCC Embedded Substrate’ Line in Vietnam… Offensive Into AI Market

Samsung Electro-Mechanics is establishing a production line for ‘MLCC (multilayer ceramic capacitor) embedded semiconductor substrates’ at its Vietnam factory. MLCC embedded semiconductor substrates integrate various passive components internally to boost performance and efficiency, and the move is seen as Samsung Electro-Mechanics making a strategic bet on the AI semiconductor substrate market.

According to industry sources on April 12, Samsung Electro-Mechanics has decided to build an MLCC embedded substrate production line at its Vietnam plant and is planning the associated capex.

The company will bring in new equipment and is preparing to collaborate with Korean substrate manufacturers with operations in Vietnam. Outsourcing certain process steps is also under review. New equipment for creating cavities inside substrates to house MLCCs has reportedly been co-developed with partners. Initial purchase orders for equipment are expected as early as this month.

An industry source familiar with the matter said, “Samsung Electro-Mechanics has begun preparations to build a large-scale MLCC embedded substrate supply chain,” adding that “investment in line buildout and a cooperative ecosystem will take place over two years.” The industry estimates hundreds of billions of won will be invested in manufacturing equipment and broader supply chain infrastructure.

MLCCs function like a dam that stores electricity and releases it in controlled amounts. Smaller than a grain of rice, they are known as the “rice of the electronics industry.” Samsung Electro-Mechanics’ MLCC embedded substrate is a product that embeds MLCCs inside the substrate itself.

Compared to the conventional approach of mounting components on top of the substrate, this method takes up less space and shortens physical distances, resulting in higher efficiency. It is advantageous for implementing high-performance semiconductor chips.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics has been supplying MLCC embedded substrates in small volumes to select customers. Through this investment, the company plans to significantly scale up production capacity.

The proliferation of AI has driven continued efforts to improve the performance of AI semiconductor chips—core infrastructure—and growing market demand for Samsung Electro-Mechanics’ MLCC embedded substrates is the backdrop for this new investment. A significant number of AI chip companies and big tech firms have reportedly already inquired with Samsung Electro-Mechanics about supply of MLCC embedded substrates.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics plans to ramp up MLCC embedded substrate supply to establish an early lead in the AI semiconductor substrate market. The MLCC embedded substrate segment is a new market with virtually no competing substrate makers.

Another industry source said, “Samsung Electro-Mechanics is also planning a strategy to embed not only MLCCs but eventually silicon capacitors inside substrates as well.”

Silicon capacitors offer 100x lower resistance than ceramic-based MLCCs, further reducing signal transmission losses while maintaining stable characteristics under high voltage and high temperatures.

text:
Rapidus Chairman Higashi: "We're investing because 2nm is achievable"

"As chairman of Rapidus, having been in this industry for a long time, I say this with the conviction that Japan must achieve 2nm no matter what."

Terry Higashi, Chairman of Rapidus (former chairman of Tokyo Electron), emphasized this during a keynote speech at the 15th Bandi Jeju Forum held at Jeju National University on April 10, hosted by the Korea Society of Display Technology (KSDT).

Rapidus disclosed that construction of the Chitose factory (IIM) in Hokkaido—targeting leading-edge 2nm process technology—is progressing smoothly toward mass production readiness. The company held the opening ceremony for its R&D building, where process technology development and prototype fabrication are being carried out, on April 11. Key equipment including EUV (extreme ultraviolet) lithography tools has also been progressively installed.

Chairman Higashi unveiled drone footage of the Rapidus facility, stating, "The R&D building is nearing completion, and the opening ceremony is scheduled for tomorrow." He added, "There are buildings for quality analysis, employee workspaces, and a utility zone for handling chemicals, with actual manufacturing activities taking place inside the fab."

Rapidus is a Japanese foundry consortium established in late 2022 with the goal of reviving Japan's semiconductor industry, funded by ¥1 billion (approximately ₩9.4 billion) contributions from each of eight founding companies: Toyota, Sony, Kioxia, NTT, SoftBank, NEC, Denso, and Mitsubishi UFJ Bank. Starting with these eight, an additional 20 or so companies—including Fujitsu, Canon, and Honda—have reportedly expressed interest in contributing, and with IBM also joining, the consortium is expected to expand to approximately 30 members this year.

Chairman Higashi noted, "From the 1980s through 1992, Japan held the world's No. 1 position with a 50% global semiconductor market share, but it has since declined to around 8% today. It's not just market share we lost—we also lost leading-edge logic semiconductor technology." He continued, "Meanwhile, the U.S. has revived its lost share, and in Asia, semiconductors have seen tremendous growth led by Korea and Taiwan."

He went on to say, "Currently, four major players—TSMC, Samsung Electronics, IBM, and Intel—are advancing semiconductor technology. The industry has progressed from planar in the 2000s to FinFET in the 2010s, and now to gate-all-around (GAA) 2nm." He added, "Japan has Renesas, which was at the 40nm level in the 2010s and remains around 40nm today."

However, recent developments show a growing trend of expanding collaboration with overseas manufacturers that have been successfully attracted to Japan, such as TSMC. Leveraging the Japanese government's large-scale subsidy programs, the strategy is to build advanced semiconductor fabs domestically and thereby expand Japan's influence in the global AI infrastructure market.

Chairman Higashi said, "Recently, TSMC has built a factory in Kyushu, Japan, working on 28/22nm, 16/12nm, and eventually 3nm production." He added, "Japan has fallen more than a decade behind the rest of the world, and it was against this backdrop that in August 2022 we decided to build 2nm GAA semiconductors. Rapidus was born from this context."

Securing 2nm Big Tech Customers Is Key — "The government is investing enormously"

Rapidus is currently devoting all its efforts to securing North American Big Tech customers based on its 2nm leading-edge process mass production capability. Internal personnel have reportedly been traveling to the U.S. to focus on business development. The company has already completed production of 2nm test wafers and is targeting mass production for external customers by 2027.

To this end, Rapidus is constructing Fab 1 (IIM-1) in Chitose, Hokkaido, with plans to add a second fab in phases. Production capacity at the time of mass production next year is expected to reach approximately 25,000–30,000 wafers per month.

Installation of key equipment for mass production readiness is also proceeding sequentially. IIM-1 has reportedly received two EUV lithography tools to date. EUV tools use 13.5nm-wavelength extreme ultraviolet light and are essential for manufacturing semiconductors at 7nm and below. Rapidus is pursuing a long-term roadmap targeting the installation of ten EUV tools.

Industry observers expect Japan to exert considerable influence in semiconductor manufacturing, leveraging its strong competitiveness in materials and equipment. Japan possesses world-leading materials technology and equipment capabilities, holding a de facto monopoly in advanced materials such as EUV photoresist (PR) essential for semiconductor fine-patterning, and Tokyo Electron (TEL) ranks among the world's top five semiconductor equipment companies.

Nevertheless, some view that even if 2nm product development and pilot production are achievable, securing meaningful market share through full-scale mass production will take time. Given that the foundry business inherently relies on years of accumulated manufacturing experience and customer trust, competing against established players like TSMC and Samsung Electronics will be extremely challenging.

Chairman Higashi concluded, "We're doing this because we truly believe 2nm is achievable, and the government is investing enormously." He emphasized, "The opposite of success is not failure—it's doing nothing. If you fail, you connect it to the next success. That's how semiconductor history has unfolded, and that's how the industry has grown."

text:
Glass Substrate Race Heats Up… Intel Targets 'Technology Standard,' Samsung Electro-Mechanics Pursues 'Customer Wins'

The commercialization race for glass substrates—widely regarded as a game changer in next-generation semiconductor packaging—has moved beyond the technology announcement phase into genuine mass-production preparation. Surging demand for high-performance AI chips has exposed the physical limits of conventional FC-BGA substrates, elevating glass substrates as a key alternative thanks to their superior thermal stability and fine-pitch wiring capabilities. Market attention is now shifting from the technology competition itself toward production timelines and monetization potential.

According to industry sources on April 10, Intel has positioned glass substrates as a core next-generation packaging technology and is moving to seize first-mover advantage. With over a decade of R&D, Intel has invested more than $1 billion in R&D and pilot infrastructure at its Chandler, Arizona facility.

The crux of Intel's technology lies in combining its proprietary advanced packaging solution, EMIB (Embedded Multi-die Interconnect Bridge), with next-generation substrate technology. EMIB is an interconnect technology that links heterogeneous dies at high speed; it has already been applied in select high-performance products, demonstrating proven scalability.

Glass substrates enable finer wiring and larger-area packaging compared to conventional materials, providing a foundation for further expanding chip-to-chip interconnect architectures. This would allow CPUs, GPUs, HBM, and other heterogeneous dies to be integrated as a single system, with expected benefits including faster data movement, reduced power loss, and improved AI compute efficiency. Building on these packaging and substrate innovations, Intel has laid out a roadmap targeting one trillion transistors per package by 2030, setting the directional framework for next-generation packaging architectures.

Notably, Intel's ambition extends beyond mere technological superiority to standard-setting. If glass-substrate-based architectures become the backbone of next-generation packaging, Intel's design and interconnect methodologies could solidify as de facto industry standards. This would effectively let Intel dictate specifications across the foundry and packaging ecosystem—a strategy interpreted as an effort to secure structural dominance in the AI semiconductor market.

That said, the technology remains at the implementation and reliability validation stage; the industry broadly expects stable high-volume manufacturing no earlier than 2027. While Intel is credited with leading on both technology and ecosystem development, the actual commercialization race is widely seen as just beginning.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics is accelerating a "customer traction" strategy alongside the technology competition. Industry sources indicate that Samsung Electro-Mechanics has recently supplied glass substrate samples to Apple in addition to Broadcom, entering the qualification lines of major global big-tech firms. The company is producing prototypes through a pilot line at its Sejong facility, targeting trial production this year followed by mass production after 2027. Where Intel leads with technology direction and ecosystem building, Samsung Electro-Mechanics aims to lock in key customer touchpoints—such as Apple—to capture commercialization wins first.

Absolics, a subsidiary of SKC, is considered the fastest mover on production infrastructure. It has established a dedicated manufacturing base in Georgia, USA, and SKC plans to allocate approximately KRW 590 billion out of roughly KRW 1 trillion raised through a rights offering toward product development and process stabilization. However, challenges remain around global customer qualification and achieving economically viable yields, and the pace of commercialization has turned somewhat more cautious relative to market expectations. Even with facilities in place, actual competitiveness is expected to hinge on process maturity and yield levels.

LG Innotek is taking a measured approach, monitoring market demand while strengthening its fundamentals. The company is bolstering core technologies through a partnership with glass precision-processing firm UTI, while building a pilot production line at a domestic facility. CEO Moon Hyuk-soo indicated a mass-production target of 2028 while noting that full-scale market demand may not materialize until around 2030—a stance interpreted as prioritizing technology readiness and market timing over an aggressive sprint.

An industry executive commented: "The glass substrate market is moving beyond R&D into a 'production competition' phase, where dominance will go to companies that can generate real revenue at stable yields. The true inflection point will come when companies clear the rigorous qualification processes of global customers and begin actual supply."

text:
SK Hynix Begins Full-Scale HBM4 DRAM Production at New M15X Fab This Month

SK Hynix is ramping up mass production of cutting-edge DRAM at its new M15X fab in Cheongju starting this month. M15X is expected to serve as the key production hub for scaling high-bandwidth memory (HBM) output through next year. While overall production scale remains smaller than the Wuxi (China) and Icheon (Korea) fabs, the company plans to maximize profits during the current super-cycle by deploying advanced process equipment en masse and accelerating the ramp-up timeline.

According to industry sources on April 10, the M15X fab will gradually increase wafer input from a monthly average of 10,000 wafers this month, targeting a maximum of 80,000 wafers per month by next year. Given the pace of equipment installation and setup this year, the line is expected to handle 30,000 to a maximum of 50,000 wafers per month by year-end — roughly two months ahead of the original schedule. The DRAM produced at M15X will be allocated primarily to high-margin products including 6th-generation HBM (HBM4), with a portion going toward high-performance server DRAM.

M15X is a new DRAM production base built through an approximately KRW 20 trillion investment to expand the existing M15 fab. Until the first fab within the Yongin semiconductor cluster is completed in 2027, M15X will serve as the primary facility for addressing next-generation HBM demand. The timeline for the Yongin cluster fab's actual commissioning remains uncertain — the industry expects it to come online next year, but sources both inside and outside SK Hynix suggest 2028 or later is more likely due to local government and infrastructure issues. This makes M15X SK Hynix's sole avenue for expanding DRAM production capacity until Yongin comes online.

M15X is a state-of-the-art line equipped with a large number of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography tools required for cutting-edge DRAM production. The industry estimates approximately KRW 12 trillion worth of EUV equipment has been deployed at M15X. The 10nm 5th-generation (1b) DRAM primarily produced on this line is expected to help increase the share of high-performance DRAM products — including HBM, server, PC, and mobile — in the product mix.

Once M15X reaches full utilization, SK Hynix's total DRAM output is expected to increase by 10–15% in wafer terms. However, the consensus is that its contribution will be far greater in terms of HBM supply capacity, revenue mix, and profitability, given the line's specialization in advanced processes. SK Hynix itself emphasized M15X as an HBM-optimized hub during its earnings call, and SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won has noted that HBM consumes far more wafers than conventional DRAM — suggesting the vast majority of output will be directed toward reinforcing HBM leadership.

The expansion of SK Hynix's DRAM production synergies — currently centered on Wuxi and Icheon — into Cheongju also carries significant implications. The M15X fab is located directly adjacent to the existing M15 fab, which is scaling up investment in through-silicon via (TSV) equipment, creating favorable conditions for HBM production optimization. TSV is a technology that enables vertical electrical connections through silicon interposers and is essential for manufacturing memory products like HBM. With M15 and M15X at its core, the Cheongju site is poised to emerge as a key HBM hub, synergizing with TSV back-end processes and future packaging investment in Cheongju.

A source close to SK Hynix explained: "M15X is a capacity expansion card that can boost SK Hynix's total DRAM wafer capacity by up to nearly 20%, but its more fundamental significance lies in being the fab that resolves the advanced DRAM bottleneck for HBM. The goal is not just incremental output gains, but filling the gap before the Yongin fab comes online to rapidly respond to the HBM market leadership race against competitors."

text:
AI chip demand tightens ABF substrate supply, three-year upcycle in sight

As AI CPUs, GPUs, and application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) advance to new generations, they are driving a sharp increase in both substrate size and layer counts. Simultaneously, supply constraints across upstream materials — including glass fiber cloth, copper foil, and drill bits — are creating bottlenecks that are gradually tilting capacity toward a supply shortfall and extending forward visibility across the IC substrate sector.

Industry sources expect ABF substrates to begin returning to a supply-demand imbalance from the first half of 2026, supported by strong demand from multiple AI customers. The gap is projected to widen further in 2027 and 2028, signaling the start of a three-year "super expansion cycle" for the IC substrate industry.

Supply chain estimates suggest that leading players — including Ibiden, Samsung Electro-Mechanics (Semco), AT&S, and Taiwan-based Unimicron, Kinsus, and Nan Ya PCB (NPC) — stand to benefit from pricing upside driven by tightening supply.

The industry had previously faced prolonged oversupply following aggressive capacity expansion after the pandemic, with excess capacity persisting for three years and continuing through the end of 2025. AI-driven increases in substrate size and complexity, however, are set to make 2026 a turning point toward supply tightness.

For example, Nvidia's next-generation platforms highlight this shift. The Vera CPU uses a substrate nearly 50% larger than that of the previous Grace platform, while the Blackwell GPU requires more than double the substrate area compared with the Hopper generation.

Looking further ahead, the Rubin GPU is expected to increase substrate area by an additional 75% over Blackwell. This trend — spanning AI CPUs and GPUs to the rapid scaling of ASIC chips — points to accelerating demand for ABF substrates, making future supply constraints increasingly likely.

Taiwan-based substrate makers note that extended lead times for copper-clad laminates (CCL), along with rising prices for glass fiber cloth, copper foil, and drill bits, have already tightened supply for high-layer-count ABF substrates. This has triggered broader price adjustments across the IC substrate market, with increases expected to accelerate in the second half of 2026 compared with the first.

Current price hikes remain more measured than during the pandemic, as the market has not yet fully entered a supply shortage phase. For now, ABF and BT substrate prices are rising at a moderate pace of around 3–7% per quarter in 2026, with adjustments applied selectively rather than across all end markets, allowing suppliers to gradually pass through cost pressures.

A key variable remains the pace of new capacity for T-glass fiber cloth, which continues to constrain overall substrate supply. Currently, around 70% of T-glass fiber cloth demand is allocated to ABF substrates, with the remaining 30% used for BT substrates.

Industry estimates indicate that shortages of T-glass fiber cloth will persist through 2027, with the supply-demand gap peaking in 2026. However, as new capacity from Japan's Nittobo, Taiwan Glass Ind. (TGI), And China's Grace Fabric comes online, the imbalance is expected to begin easing in 2027.

text:
Samsung Electronics Mobile: Q2 Is the 'Real Crunch'… Concerns Over a Swing to Operating Loss

Samsung Electronics' Mobile eXperience (MX) division posted better-than-expected profitability in Q1. This is attributed to price hikes on new products and the use of existing memory semiconductor inventory to contain cost increases as much as possible.

However, memory semiconductor prices have continued to rise sharply into Q2, adding to the burden on the smartphone industry. As a result, concerns are emerging that Samsung's MX division could swing to an operating loss as early as this quarter.

According to industry sources on April 9, MX division profitability is expected to decline significantly quarter-over-quarter in Q2.

Samsung Electronics' preliminary results released on April 7 showed revenue of KRW 133 trillion and operating profit of KRW 57.2 trillion. Of this, MX division operating profit is estimated at KRW 3–4 trillion — well above the industry consensus of KRW 2 trillion-range.

The strong results were driven by multiple factors. The industry had initially expected MX to be hit hard by rising LPDDR prices and growing IT market uncertainty stemming from the war.

In response, Samsung raised prices on the Galaxy S26 flagship launched in Q1 to defend profitability. The company also reportedly drew down existing memory inventory to suppress cost increases as much as possible.

Still, the consensus view is that the impact of rising memory prices will be unavoidable in Q2. LPDDR prices have been climbing sharply every quarter, and the inventory drawdown strategy is difficult to sustain. In a worst-case scenario, MX could swing to a loss within the quarter.

An IT industry official noted: "MX's Q1 profitability came in far above expectations, so the base effect in Q2 will be significant. Given the continued rise in DRAM prices through Q2, the possibility of a swing to loss cannot be ruled out."

The DRAM market has been facing acute supply tightness as global IT companies aggressively expand AI infrastructure spending. At the same time, memory suppliers have been shifting production mix toward higher-margin server DRAM and HBM. NVIDIA-led demand for server LPDDR has also increased. As a result, the supply-demand imbalance for LPDDR used in smartphones and other IT devices has been worsening.

For example, Apple saw LPDDR prices from Samsung and SK Hynix roughly double QoQ in Q1. In Q2, an additional price increase of at least 50% QoQ is understood to be under discussion.

Samsung's MX division faces a similar level of memory price increases. While it has the structural advantage of sourcing DRAM internally through the Device Solutions (DS) division, it is difficult to deviate significantly from market pricing. If DS were to supply DRAM to MX at excessively low prices, it could raise concerns over preferential treatment.

Samsung and SK Hynix: NAND Utilization Rates Recover as Lineups Shift Toward High-Performance Products

Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are expected to generate massive profits from their NAND flash businesses this year. The surge is driven by rising solid-state drive (SSD) demand fueled by expanding AI data center investment, which has sharply boosted NAND sales volumes. Both companies plan to rapidly transition their NAND lineups toward high-performance products in line with this trend.

According to sell-side consensus, the two companies' combined NAND operating profit is projected to reach approximately KRW 11.6 trillion this year—roughly KRW 7.2 trillion for Samsung and KRW 4.4 trillion for SK Hynix. This represents increases of 26.8x and 12.6x year-over-year, respectively.

Both companies have already posted strong NAND profits starting in Q1. In Samsung's preliminary earnings released on April 7, the DS (Device Solutions) division's operating profit was estimated at approximately KRW 5.4 trillion, of which NAND is believed to have contributed around KRW 1.25 trillion—roughly 23% of the total. This marks a clear turnaround from the KRW 300 billion operating loss recorded in Q1 of last year.

Expectations are also high for SK Hynix, which is set to report earnings on April 23. The Q1 operating profit consensus for SK Hynix stands at approximately KRW 3.1 trillion, with NAND estimated to account for the mid-KRW 400 billion range (~15%).

Originally, neither company had placed significant emphasis on their NAND businesses. Samsung had even been reviewing the possibility of converting parts of its NAND production lines to commodity DRAM. However, as AI data center CAPEX expanded and hard disk drive (HDD) supply shortages intensified, demand for SSDs—as a substitute—surged. This rapidly increased NAND sales volumes for both Samsung and SK Hynix, reversing market sentiment.

Utilization rates at both companies have also improved significantly. An SK Hynix official stated, "Starting from early this year, NAND fab utilization rates rose sharply, reaching as high as 98% at one point. We are even redeploying equipment that had previously been underutilized." Samsung is also reported to have recovered NAND fab utilization at its Xi'an and Pyeongtaek facilities to approximately 80%.

In particular, demand for high-performance quad-level cell (QLC)-based enterprise SSDs (eSSDs) is growing rapidly. Industry sources claim that major memory makers have already sold out their QLC NAND inventory, including lower-spec products.

Samsung and SK Hynix are accelerating conversion investments toward their next-generation 9th-generation V9 QLC products (286 layers for Samsung, 321 layers for SK Hynix). The V9 QLC is expected to become the flagship lineup for both companies this year. An industry source noted, "For 9th-gen NAND, SK Hynix is more aggressive than Samsung. Its conversion investment pace is currently the fastest."

Both companies are also investing in next-generation roadmaps. Discussion has already moved beyond QLC to penta-level cell (PLC). NAND is categorized by the number of bits stored per cell—SLC (1-bit), MLC (2-bit), TLC (3-bit), QLC (4-bit), and PLC (5-bit)—with higher bit counts enabling greater storage density per unit area.

SK Hynix is currently the more active player in PLC development. The company presented research findings at IEDM 2025 in the U.S. late last year, demonstrating a multi-site cell (MSC) architecture that achieves 5-bit storage by splitting a cell into two sites and combining voltage states—suggesting a viable path toward PLC commercialization. Samsung has disclosed limited information publicly regarding PLC.

However, the industry largely expects PLC commercialization to be delayed beyond initial expectations. At CES 2026, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang introduced the concept of "Inference Context Memory Storage (ICMS)," and the NAND required for ICMS is seen as prioritizing speed over storage density.

A semiconductor industry source explained, "Since speed is the core requirement for ICMS, adopting QLC and TLC—which are capable of high-speed operation—is the realistic choice. PLC requires entirely new device, process, and circuit designs, so the gap between SK Hynix's research presentation and actual productization is significant."

text:
One-year contracts are a thing of the past… Samsung and SK hynix won't sell without 3–5 year long-term supply agreements

Samsung Electronics and SK hynix have effectively abandoned the practice of signing one-year short-term memory supply contracts with global big tech companies, opting instead to supply products exclusively through 3–5 year long-term agreements (LTAs). The strategy aims to build a stable, high-margin business model through strategic collaboration with customers from the earliest stages of AI memory development.

According to industry sources on the 8th, Samsung Electronics has established a policy of applying a minimum three-year LTA to all new contracts starting this year. Until last year, the company had been accommodating even quarterly ultra-short-term contracts, but has now decided to fully transition its supply policy to an LTA framework. At the annual general meeting on March 18, Samsung Electronics DS Division CEO (Vice Chairman) Jeon Young-hyun stated: "We are pursuing a shift in supply contracts with our customers from the current annual and quarterly basis to multi-year agreements spanning 3–5 years." Accordingly, Samsung is expected to secure stable three-year memory supply commitments with major customers including AMD — with which negotiations are in the final stages — as well as Microsoft and Google.

Furthermore, SK hynix has reportedly been pursuing a five-year commodity DRAM long-term supply agreement with Google. While a three-year term was initially considered the leading option, an internal assessment that "even three years is too short" led to a decision to extend the contract period to five years to maximize supply stability. Given that SK hynix is currently the primary supplier of 5th-generation High Bandwidth Memory (HBM3E) to Google, the company is said to be negotiating an additional two-year extension by leveraging next-generation HBM supply as a condition. Negotiations that were originally slated for completion by year-end are now expected to be finalized within the first half.

Historically, the memory market was built on commoditization. Commodity DRAM for PCs and smartphones was mass-produced and sold based on quarterly fixed transaction prices or daily-fluctuating spot prices. As a result, even slight demand fluctuations triggered price collapses, leading to trillion-won-scale losses — the inescapable "curse of the cycle." Suppliers were unilaterally exposed to market conditions in a classic subordinate position.

By contrast, a shift to an LTA framework minimizes the risk of order cliffs. By locking in volumes for three to five-plus years, companies can defend earnings with pre-committed prices and volumes even amid demand shocks from economic downturns — effectively securing downside rigidity where profits no longer plunge during downturns. Samsung Electronics is reportedly reviewing supply pricing policies to hedge against DRAM price volatility alongside minimum annual supply volume provisions as part of the LTA transition.

The shift is also effective from a capital expenditure efficiency standpoint. With volumes already committed, disciplined and calculated CAPEX becomes possible, replacing reckless capacity expansion races. The semiconductor industry expects that as the share of long-term contracts rises, memory companies' margins will stabilize at levels structurally higher than in the past. In particular, for products like HBM — where process complexity is high and customer requirements vary — a made-to-order supply system based on "secure orders first, produce after," akin to the foundry model, is essential to eliminate inventory risk at the source and maximize production efficiency.

An industry official commented: "The era of memory companies anxiously stockpiling inventory while worrying about price declines is over. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix have now been elevated beyond mere memory suppliers to strategic infrastructure partners for global big tech."

text:
China's CXMT to Mass-Produce 12-High HBM3/HBM3E Next Year… Closing In on Korea

China is pushing to mass-produce 12-high HBM just three years after entering the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) market. This is the highest stack count currently commercialized, suggesting China has secured the technology for mainstream products led by Korean companies. The consensus is that China is emerging as a new threat, narrowing the technology gap year by year.

According to industry sources on April 8, China's largest memory manufacturer CXMT is set to begin mass production of 12-high HBM next year. The company is reportedly in discussions with domestic and foreign materials, components, and equipment suppliers on capital expenditure plans.

An industry insider familiar with the matter said, "CXMT is entering mass production of 4th-generation 'HBM3 8-high' this year while simultaneously beginning full-scale discussions with partners for 12-high HBM production. Technology upgrades and equipment investments for DRAM stacking will follow."

12-high is currently the highest stack count for HBM mounted on AI semiconductor chips, with the majority of market supply being HBM3E 12-high. SK Hynix, Samsung Electronics, and Micron hold market share in that order. HBM4 — which Samsung began mass-producing in February (with SK Hynix and Micron also pursuing supply) — is also initially being supplied as a 12-high product.

HBM increases bandwidth (speed) by vertically stacking DRAM, and the number of layers stacked serves as a key measure of technological capability. The technical difficulty of attaching micro bumps (solder balls) to connect upper and lower DRAM layers and bonding them without error is high. Thermal management after stacking is also required — this is why yields (the ratio of good units) drop when manufacturing DRAM into HBM.

CXMT's moves are evidence that it has resolved these technical challenges to a certain extent. Notably, the gap with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix has narrowed further. CXMT began mass production of 2nd-generation 'HBM2 4-high' in H2 2024. At the time, the technology gap was considered large, as SK Hynix had already entered mass production of HBM3E 12-high.

However, the situation is reversing as CXMT challenges mainstream 12-high mass production roughly three years after its full market entry — it has already caught up to within striking distance of Korean HBM. The industry consensus is that the Korea-China HBM technology gap has shrunk to three years or less.

'Helium Crisis' Comes to a Close... Samsung and SK Hynix Secure Long-Term U.S. Supply Contracts

The semiconductor-grade helium supply anxiety triggered by the Iran war has been largely resolved.

German-based Linde and U.S.-based Air Products — both of which source and refine helium feedstock from the United States for semiconductor use — have reportedly signed long-term supplementary supply contracts with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.

According to industry sources on April 8, Linde and Air Products committed to fully addressing helium supply shortages for Samsung and SK Hynix following Iran's airstrike on Qatar's Ras Laffan complex, entering into separate long-term agreements. Both companies source a large share of their raw helium domestically in the U.S., leaving them largely unaffected by the Qatar-originating supply disruption.

Prior to the war, helium was reportedly in a state of mild oversupply. Linde and Air Products moved quickly as procurement disruption fears spread due to the Iran conflict, effectively capitalizing on the situation. An industry source explained, "Linde and Air Products not only filled the supply gap but also secured additional long-term supply contracts on top of that." Samsung and SK Hynix are also reported to have accepted the helium price increases that arose during the crisis response.

France's Air Liquide and Japan's Iwatani, both heavily dependent on Qatari helium, were unintentionally hit hard by the war. Industry observers note that this event is likely to trigger a restructuring of Korea's semiconductor helium procurement network toward U.S.-sourced supply.

The Blue House also issued an official statement on the helium supply situation on April 7. Policy Chief Kim Yong-beom said at a press briefing, "We have been informed that approximately four months' worth of helium has been secured," adding, "We have been briefed that there are no issues over the medium term." A senior Blue House official noted that the secured volumes are U.S.-sourced.

On March 31, the Korea Semiconductor Industry Association also stated, "Domestic semiconductor companies have pre-secured a certain level of inventory for all necessary raw materials including helium," and that "individual companies operate multiple procurement channels, so the likelihood of short-term supply instability is also low."

Helium is used in semiconductor manufacturing as a key gas in plasma etching and deposition processes, and also serves as a backside wafer coolant.

Helium is a byproduct extracted during LNG production, with Qatar accounting for roughly one-third of global supply. Iran had previously carried out multiple strikes on Qatar's Ras Laffan industrial complex. When QatarEnergy declared that damage to its LNG production facilities would make it difficult to fulfill long-term supply contracts, concerns over helium procurement disruptions spread across the semiconductor industry.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics Secures FC-BGA Supply for 'Groq 3 LPU,' Enters NVIDIA Supply Chain

Samsung Electro-Mechanics has secured a leading position in the supply chain for semiconductor package substrates used in the Groq 3 Language Processing Unit (LPU).

The Groq 3 LPU is an inference accelerator chip designed to enhance the performance of NVIDIA's cutting-edge AI semiconductor platform, Vera Rubin. As inference grows in importance within the AI industry, Samsung Electro-Mechanics is expected to expand its footprint within NVIDIA's AI semiconductor ecosystem.

According to a ZDNet Korea report on April 8, Samsung Electro-Mechanics has recently begun preparations for mass production of flip-chip ball grid array (FC-BGA) substrates for the Groq 3 LPU.

The company has secured "first vendor" status (top supplier by volume) for Groq 3 LPU FC-BGA substrates, with full-scale mass production expected to begin in Q2 of this year.

The Groq 3 LPU is a 4nm process-based AI inference accelerator chip, fabricated at Samsung Foundry. Samsung Foundry's wafer allocation for the Groq 3 LPU is estimated at approximately 10,000 wafers per month.

FC-BGA is a package substrate that connects semiconductor chips to the substrate using a "flip-chip bump" method. It offers superior electrical and thermal characteristics compared to conventional wire bonding.

While initial volumes are modest, this FC-BGA supply win allows Samsung Electro-Mechanics to expand its presence within NVIDIA's AI semiconductor ecosystem.

Earlier this year, Samsung Electro-Mechanics had already entered NVIDIA's supply chain by securing FC-BGA supply for the NVSwitch chip, which is used to interconnect multiple GPUs within servers. As the Groq LPU has also been adopted into NVIDIA's AI semiconductor platform, shipment volumes are expected to grow going forward.

On this topic, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang announced changes to the company's advanced AI semiconductor platform during his keynote at GTC 2026, held on March 16 (local time) in San Jose, California.

NVIDIA's Vera Rubin platform, slated for release in the second half of this year, was originally composed of six chips: the Rubin GPU, Vera CPU, BlueField-4 DPU, switches, and others. However, CEO Jensen Huang added the Groq 3 LPU, expanding the platform to a seven-chip architecture.

The approach integrates the Groq 3 LPX — an inference-dedicated rack equipped with 256 Groq 3 LPUs — into the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NV72 rack, which comprises 72 Rubin GPUs and 36 Vera CPUs.

The Groq 3 LPU is equipped with SRAM, which has lower capacity than DRAM but offers faster data transfer speeds. This significantly reduces the latency that occurred in conventional single-GPU systems during the inference stage of LLMs. According to NVIDIA, Vera Rubin combined with LPX can deliver up to 35x higher throughput per megawatt on trillion-parameter models.

To this end, NVIDIA has been building an aggressive partnership framework, including an indirect acquisition of Groq for approximately KRW 29 trillion (~$21 billion) late last year.

An industry source noted, "NVIDIA is intensifying its strategy of building an entire AI platform with chips specialized for each domain. Groq LPU adoption volumes are expected to increase further, and partner companies will benefit accordingly."

Driven by a surge in memory prices, Samsung Electronics recorded approximately KRW 10 trillion in operating profit from its NAND flash business — the highest quarterly result since the company entered the NAND business. The industry expects NAND price increases to continue, with Samsung projected to generate over KRW 50 trillion in NAND operating profit for the full year. Samsung announced preliminary results on April 7, reporting Q1 2026 revenue of KRW 133 trillion and operating profit of KRW 57.2 trillion. QoQ, revenue rose 41.73% and operating profit surged 185%. YoY, revenue increased 68.06% and operating profit jumped 755.01%.

Q1 results were driven by memory price increases, with both DRAM and NAND prices continuing to rise on the back of AI demand. The industry estimates Samsung recorded over KRW 50 trillion in operating profit from memory alone.

DRAM profitability improved further this year, with an estimated ~80% of Samsung's total Q1 operating profit attributed to DRAM. DRAM remains the biggest bottleneck in the AI industry — memory makers are pursuing capacity expansions, but physical space constraints mean meaningful additions will take considerable time.

NAND showed even steeper improvement, fueled by surging enterprise SSD (eSSD) demand. Securities analysts estimate Samsung posted ~KRW 10 trillion in NAND operating profit in Q1, compared to just over KRW 2 trillion for the entirety of last year.

Until last year, NAND was considered a business where even 10% operating margins were difficult to achieve. With more manufacturers (Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron, Kioxia, SanDisk, YMTC) than in DRAM, price competition was fierce, and NAND was relatively sidelined from AI investment, limiting demand growth.

This demand shift accelerated as inference grew in share within the AI industry. The transition from training-centric to inference-centric workloads has elevated the importance of data storage and processing architectures, driving rapid growth in NAND-based storage demand and a sharp rise in NAND ASPs. Some in the industry now forecast NAND operating margins exceeding 60% in H2.

Additionally, NVIDIA's newly unveiled ICMS (Interconnect and Memory Subsystem) is expected to further boost NAND demand. ICMS stores and utilizes KV cache generated during inference in storage rather than HBM, improving overall system compute efficiency.

Samsung had been conservative on NAND capacity expansion in recent years, focusing instead on technology migration. A source with close knowledge of Samsung said, "As NAND conditions improve, Samsung is reviewing NAND line expansion at its new P5 fab," adding that "investment scale is expected to be finalized in H2 this year."

text:
Exclusive: Samsung Electro-Mechanics Supplies Glass Substrate Samples to Apple

Samsung Electro-Mechanics has supplied semiconductor glass substrate samples to Apple. Following custom AI chip designer Broadcom, the company is now supplying samples to end-customer Apple as well, drawing assessments that it is rapidly expanding the scope of its new business.

According to reporting by The Elec as of April 7, Samsung Electro-Mechanics has been confirmed to have been supplying glass substrate samples to Apple since last year. The samples are substrate products in which the organic-material core used in conventional flip-chip ball grid array (FC-BGA) has been replaced with glass. Glass offers higher surface flatness compared to organic materials, enabling finer circuit patterning. Its lower coefficient of thermal expansion also suppresses warpage caused by thermal expansion mismatches between the chip and substrate. As AI semiconductors continue to grow in die size due to performance competition, larger substrates exacerbate warpage issues — leading many companies to consider glass substrates a critical element for next-generation products.

Broadcom is the largest potential customer for Samsung Electro-Mechanics' glass substrate business. Broadcom is the market leader in custom AI chips, co-developing AI server chips with Big Tech firms such as Google, Meta, and OpenAI, and converting those designs into foundry-manufacturable form.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics has been supplying glass core substrate samples to Broadcom since last year. If it secures the Broadcom supply, its glass substrates would be mounted on Big Tech companies' custom AI chips.

Apple also collaborates with Broadcom on AI server chips. The Information reported in December 2024 that Apple is developing its own AI server chip with Broadcom. Internally codenamed "Baltra," the chip is expected to be manufactured at TSMC fabs.

Industry observers cite two main reasons why Apple is separately sourcing and evaluating glass substrate samples directly from Samsung Electro-Mechanics, apart from Broadcom. In the near term, Apple likely wants to directly assess the packaging material characteristics that will be applied to the Broadcom platform from the perspective of the end customer. In the longer term, some interpret this as Apple laying the groundwork to eventually handle AI server chip packaging in-house using glass substrates. Apple has a track record of bringing externally sourced components — mobile application processors (APs), GPU IP, modems — in-house through its own design efforts.

Either way, winning Apple would be a major positive for Samsung Electro-Mechanics.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics is currently operating a glass substrate pilot line at its Sejong facility in South Chungcheong Province, targeting mass production from 2027 onward. In November last year, it signed an MOU with Japan's Sumitomo Chemical Group to establish a joint venture for manufacturing glass cores, a key material for glass substrates. The JV is expected to be finalized in the second half of this year, with full-scale equipment investment to follow.

An industry source said, "The customer base secured through the existing FC-BGA business can be directly carried over to the glass substrate business," adding, "Glass substrates are still an early-stage market without established standards — the key is not speed to mass production, but building trust by delivering the quality and specifications customers demand."

- Supply shortages are already spreading across high-end materials—from glass fiber fabrics to copper foils—as well as production equipment, emerging as key bottlenecks in the supply chain.

- For CCL manufacturers, lead times for both materials and equipment are extending simultaneously, creating additional challenges.

- Rising raw material prices and equipment delivery delays are forcing companies to adjust their capex pacing and plan capacity investments earlier to mitigate supply uncertainty.

- Looking at Taiwanese manufacturers, EMC announced an expansion plan to add production facilities across three sites within two years.

Helium Crisis for Semiconductors… Blue House: "Secured 4 Months' Supply from U.S., No Medium-Term Issues"

Amid growing raw material supply concerns stemming from the Middle East war, the Blue House said on April 7 that approximately four months' worth of semiconductor-grade helium has been secured from the United States and other sources, stating there are "no medium-term issues." Qatar's LNG production facilities, which account for 65% of Korea's helium imports, were hit by Iranian strikes, but alternative supply lines have since been secured through separate contracts.

Kim Yong-beom, the Blue House Chief Policy Secretary, said at a press briefing, "I've been told that roughly four months' worth [of usable reserves] of helium has been secured," adding, "This is an extremely important matter, and I've been briefed that there are no medium-term concerns for now." He also noted, "Given the four months' supply now secured, the industry has sufficient time, so we expect they will be able to lock in alternative import sources going forward."

A senior Blue House official said the helium contracted this time is U.S.-sourced. Kim also said, "We have not yet received any requests from the industry asking the government for help due to a 'helium shortage.'"

Korea's existing U.S. helium import share stands at around 28%, less than half that of Qatar (64.7%). The U.S., along with Qatar, is considered one of the world's largest helium exporters. Russia and Algeria also hold reserves. However, the U.S. consumes most of its production domestically. In 2024, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) halted all sales of federal helium reserves and transferred them to private companies.

Helium, extracted as a byproduct of gas production, is a critical raw material in semiconductor manufacturing. With no viable substitutes, and given the difficulty of storage, transportation, and processing, the global semiconductor industry has been worried about supply disruptions since Iran struck QatarEnergy's LNG facilities on March 20. QatarEnergy has stated that helium exports will decline by at least 14% due to the war, and that facility restoration could take up to five years.

There are some intriguing signs that help gauge how far China's lithography equipment technology has advanced.

According to JoongAng Ilbo's on-site interviews with SMEE representatives at SEMICON China, SMEE's DUV lithography equipment currently has the following characteristics:

- For wafer stage drive mechanisms, SMEE uses a direct-drive system rather than ball screws. This is the same approach used by ASML and is generally considered faster and more precise than ball screw configurations.
- The claimed process coverage ranges from 100nm down to the 10nm node.
- The equipment has already entered mass production and is being sold to customers.

An SMEE employee also described the equipment to visitors on the show floor as follows:

"This is a dual-stage scanning lithography system that we developed 100% in-house. Two wafer stages alternate scanning operations, and when an argon fluoride (ArF) excimer laser fires light from above, an optical system precisely controls it to form circuit patterns on the wafer."

If these claims are accurate, it would mean China has not only completed development of a DUV lithography tool capable of addressing nodes down to the 10nm range, but has already moved into mass production and commercial sales.

In particular, when you piece together the references to an ArF excimer laser, dual-stage scanning, and direct-drive architecture, the equipment appears to be a fairly advanced DUV system. If the claimed 10nm-range capability refers to critical layers, it becomes difficult to rule out the possibility that this is an ArF immersion (ArFi)-class tool. In other words, this suggests China has either come very close to state-of-the-art DUV lithography — or, in certain areas, may have already crossed that threshold.
